events.title: CRLP Fall 2026 Teacher Leadership Invitational
events.description: The California Reading and Literature Project (CRLP) hosts the 2026 Fall Teacher Leadership Invitational at UC Berkeley, centered on the theme Beyond Decoding: Unlocking Understanding. Designed for Bay Area Teacher Leaders, this event focuses on the body of research surrounding language comprehension and its role in developing skilled, engaged readers. The program examines evidence-based practices that assist students in transitioning from accurate word reading to deep, meaningful text comprehension.Program Topics & HighlightsEvidence-Based Practices: Approaches for improving language comprehension. Student Motivation: Strategies for supporting engagement during reading comprehension instruction. Core Comprehension Skills: Focus on inferencing and the structural role of language in reading comprehension. Featured Guest: An introduction to UC Berkeley Professor Kristin Keane, CRLP's Principal Investigator and co-author of Language and Literacy Beyond Decoding (the selected text for this year's Book Study). Professional Networking: Opportunities for regional literacy educators to connect and collaborate.

events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. The show examines how a Mexico City-based artists collective, the Taller de Gráfica Popular (Workshop for Popular Graphic Art), built an artistic legacy, tracing its roots from José Guadalupe Posada's portrayals of everyday Mexican life, to its enduring influence on artists on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border today.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.description: Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the VIDRINE present four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light's BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels.Featured Artworks: Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner — AnointedMichael Light — BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023Michael Pinsky — MammothDavid Buckland �� Bikini TextsAbout Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley (http://ourlifeishere.org)In 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with Marshallese youth and elders. This expedition—organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, with support from Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell—was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. Throughout 2026–27, the project runs across campus in exhibitions at Doe Library, Giannini Hall, Memorial Glade, Worth Ryder, and BAMPFA, along with courses and public programs. It culminates in an exhibition of original works at the David Brower Center, September 2027 – February 2028. ourlifeishere.org (https://art.berkeley.edu/ourlifeishere.org)About Worth Ryder Art Gallery / VIDRINE (https://art.berkeley.edu/gallery)The Worth Ryder Art Gallery (WRAG) is an educational art space that has served as a cultural and artistic resource and community center for undergraduate and graduate students, faculty, alumni, and the Bay Area community since 1960, and is a central social and artistic hub of the UC Berkeley Department of Art Practice. The gallery supports students in exhibiting their artwork in a professional gallery context, serves as an exhibition platform for emerging contemporary artistic strategies, and brings challenging and thought-provoking artwork to the UC Berkeley campus. It is named after painter and founding chair of the department, Worth Ryder. VIDRINE is Worth Ryder Art Gallery's ancillary space showcasing video, digital art, and installation. It is located around the corner from the Worth Ryder Art Gallery in the lobby of the Anthropology and Art Building.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Marius Wernig: Human iPS cell-derived microtissues to study neurodegenerative disease
events.description: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and embryonic stem cells (ESCs) have become valuable tools to investigate disease mechanisms because they can be differentiated into various somatic cell types, including those of the central nervous system (CNS), which are difficult to obtain from primary sources. Microglia are the immune cells of the central nervous system and are thought to be key players in both physiological and disease conditions. Several microglial features are poorly conserved between mice and human, such as the function of the neurodegeneration-associated immune receptor Trem2. iPSC-derived microglia offer a powerful opportunity to generate and study human microglia. However, human iPSC-derived microglia often exhibit activated phenotypes in vitro, and assessing their impact on other brain cell types remains challenging due to limitations in current co-culture systems. We developed fully defined brain microtissues, composed of human iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, co-cultured in 2D or 3D formats. Our microtissues are stable and self-sufficient over time, requiring no exogenous cytokines or growth factors. All three cell types exhibit morphologies characteristic of their in vivo environment and show functional properties. Co-cultured microglia develop more homeostatic phenotypes compared to microglia exposed to exogenous cytokines. Hence, these tri-cultures provide a unique approach to investigate cell-cell interactions between brain cell types. We found that astrocytes and not neurons are sufficient for microglial survival and maturation, and that astrocyte-derived M-CSF is essential for microglial survival. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing analyses nominated a network of reciprocal communication between cell types. Brain microtissues faithfully recapitulated pathogenic α-synuclein seeding and aggregation, suggesting their usefulness as human cell models to study not only normal but also pathological cell biological processes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Managing AI Intellectual Property at UC Berkeley
events.description: This webinar explores the challenges and opportunities of managing intellectual property for innovations involving artificial intelligence, including practical guidance for Berkeley researchers considering commercialization of their AI innovations. Across campus, AI has proliferated as a tool in research and an underlying technology of intellectual property (IP). However, in comparison to conventional device and method-based patents, AI IP has different attributes that impact its patenting and licensing potential. Likewise, in comparison to copyrightable software, AI IP often includes weights and data as well as code. Those differences require new approaches to managing, patenting, licensing, and commercializing AI IP. Bring your questions! Hosted by the UC Berkeley Office of Technology Licensing, in the Office of Intellectual Property and Industry Research Alliances. Learn about intellectual property protection on the IPIRA website (https://ipira.berkeley.edu/researchers/intellectual-property-protection). SpeakerMike Cohen is director of innovation ecosystem development at UC Berkeley. In this role, he develops initiatives and agreements that support the commercialization of university innovations and the funding of campus research. He works with faculty, students, startup companies, corporations, entrepreneurs, investors, and attorneys to advance technology transfer and new venture creation. Mike has worked with hundreds of startups and has led the patenting and licensing of more than 100 innovations across fields including biofuels, medical devices, nanotechnologies, novel materials, photovoltaics, robotics, semiconductors, software, smart grid technologies, wireless sensors, and biomimetic systems. Mike is the author of Startup Campus: How UC Berkeley Became an Unexpected Leader in Entrepreneurship and Startups (2025).

events.title: Plant evolutionary adventures in photosynthesis
events.description: The field of phylogenetic biology emerged several decades ago, and it is an opportune time to reflect on how it has matured. On the one hand, the development of public databases and increased computing power have enabled phylogenetic studies to become impressively broad and global in scope. At the same time, and in the background, collaborative teams have, over many years, developed deeply integrative research programs that are focused intensely on a particular clade of organisms. We have recently delineated this approach, which we term "clade biology", as an exceptionally valuable subdiscipline of phylogenetic biology, providing unique insights and opportunities that taxonomically broader, global approaches cannot. Within this framework, I'll present our 25 years of work with the plant clade Portulacineae, which includes the cacti and their fascinating relatives. Our sustained focus on this clade has enabled some key discoveries, particularly regarding the evolution of alternative photosynthetic pathways in plants. In this talk I'll present two case studies. Several years ago, in our work with purslane (Portulaca), we identified and described an entirely new kind of photosynthetic metabolism, what we call "C4+CAM"- and we believe it likely that this metabolism has evolved in other lineages. More recently in our work in Californian and South American Cistantheae, we have just identified the first unequivocal evolutionary losses of CAM photosynthesis, providing a new system for understanding how and why adaptive traits are lost.

events.title: 100 Years Later: The Role of the University of California in the Loss of Ohlone Land Rights and Steps Toward Repair
events.location: 'ottoytak located on the Patio of the Hearst Museum
events.description: 100 Years Later: The Role of the University of California in the Loss of Ohlone Land Rights and Steps Toward Repair 'ottoy is a Chochenyo word and an Ohlone philosophy for repair. In 1925, the University erroneously declared the Ohlone people extinct, subsequently and unjustly leading to the loss of land rights for the Verona Band of Alameda County. A century later, the campus-wide 'ottoy Initiative is expanding throughout campus as it uplifts Ohlone culture and knowledge in a truthful and legitimate manner. Join 'ottoy Initiative leaders Vincent Medina and Louis Trevino as they discuss this historic initiative that points to a new way forward in repair between the University and the East Bay Ohlone people. Brownies and tea will be provided. This is the first in a series of educational talks sponsored by Native American Thriving Initiatives focusing on Ohlone people. This partnership between Native American Thriving Initiatives and the 'ottoy Initiative seeks to provide public education on contemporary and historical issues impacting East Bay Ohlone people.

events.title: Book Talk: Global Racism – A Challenge for the World
events.description: Join the Miller Institute for Global Challenges and the Law and the Thelton E. Henderson Center for Social Justice in welcoming Professor Anna Spain Bradley (Distinguished MacArthur Foundation Chair in International Justice and Human Rights, Professor of Law at UCLA School of Law) to UC Berkeley Law. In this lunchtime conversation, Prof. Spain Bradley will discuss her forthcoming book Global Racism: A Challenge for the World. Executive Director Savala Nolan will moderate. All in attendance will be entered in a raffle to receive a free signed copy of the book. For more information about Prof. Spain Bradley and her work, go to her website here: https://annaspainbradley.com/ (https://annaspainbradley.com/)This event is open to all. Lunch will be served inside of Room 170 starting at 12:50 PM. RSVPs will be prioritized. RSVP Here (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/book-talk-global-racism-a-challenge-for-the-world-tickets-2002471819116?aff=oddtdtcreator)From Website:Anna Spain Bradley is an author, award-winning legal scholar, higher education leader, and globally recognized human rights expert. She holds the MacArthur Foundation Chair in International Justice and Human Rights and is a Professor of Law at UCLA School of Law. With two decades of experience studying the role of law in promoting peace, dignity, and human rights around the world, she has devoted over ten years to leadership roles in higher education, including as UCLA's Vice Chancellor for Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion.Her latest book, Global Racism: A Challenge for the World, (Oxford University Press, October 2026), articulates the phenomenon of global racism as a universally available form of oppression operating on a global scale that interacts with the human ecosystem and world order. Global racism poses a serious threat to humanity, capable of existing anywhere and everywhere. Professor Spain Bradley takes readers on a journey across continents and centuries, reimagining the fight against racism as a fight for our shared humanity. Jared Diamond, Pulitzer Prize-winning author of Guns, Germs, and Steel, writes, "This powerful, compelling book exposes racism as a global phenomenon. It thrives in countries from Albania to the USA. It targets peoples from Asians and Africans to Jews, Roma, and Ukrainians. You'll come to realize: in today's globalized world, racism imperils not only its victims, but also its perpetrators."Global Racism builds upon Professor Spain Bradley's pioneering legal scholarship "Human Rights Racism" (Harvard Human Rights Journal, 2019) identifying racism as an undefined violation of human rights under international law. Her first book Human Choice in International Law (Cambridge University Press, 2021) challenges traditional assumptions about rationality in legal decision making by introducing insights from neuroscience to the study of international legal and political decision making.

events.description: NOTE: 2 speakers for this day.Kamalini RamdasDeloitte Chair in Innovation and Entrepreneurship; Professor of Management Science and Operations BSc (Delhi) MSc (Delaware) PhD (Wharton) Kamalini's main research interest is in identifying radical service delivery innovations that expand access to essential life-improving services and in finding ways to increase their adoption, especially in underprivileged populations. events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - Anil Seth (Utah)
events.description: Title: Lessons from our Nearest Galaxy NucleusAbstract: Omega Centauri is the most massive star cluster in the Milky Way, and there is strong evidence it was once the nucleus of a dwarf galaxy that fell into the Milky Way, making it the nearest galaxy nucleus. This makes it a model object for understanding the massive black holes and dense nuclear star clusters that form in galaxy centers. This talk will focus on recent results from the oMEGACat survey (https://omegacatalog.github.io/), including the strong evidence for an intermediate mass black hole and our effort to measure its mass updated mass estimates. I will also discuss our comprehensive census of stellar age and helium abundances, and the first detection of one of the roughly 10,000 stellar mass black holes expected to reside in the cluster.Host: Dan Weisz

events.title: Mona Fawaz: Planning Amid Division — The Politics of the "Public" in Beirut | City & Regional Planning Lecture
events.description: Mona Fawaz interrogates the normative foundations of progressive planning, particularly its assumption that participatory and co-productive practices can yield inclusive planning responses. She does so against a global rise in right-wing populist politics that has unsettled assumptions about a functional public. Once grounded in a belief in a shared interest, planning now operates within an increasingly fragmented political and epistemic landscape (Rivero et al., 2020). Populist discourses have deepened social divisions and eroded the state's legitimacy as custodian of the common good. Concurrently, the post-truth era further complicates co-production by destabilizing expert knowledge — the foundation on which scholars engage communities (Perry 2020). These political and epistemic ruptures expose the limits of consensus-driven planning, echoing Chantal Mouffe's (2005) critique of the "post-political" denial of conflict. Fawaz examines these dynamics through a case study of a public intervention in Beirut, Lebanon, following the 2020 Port explosion. Researchers affiliated with the Beirut Urban Lab attempted to co-design a public square, confronting tensions between knowledge, politics, and representation in a post-truth environment. Drawing on this work, Fawaz reflects on how co-production might be reimagined, proposing pathways for reintegrating power, acknowledging conflict, and rethinking a fractured public within planning. About Mona Fawaz is professor of urban studies and planning at the American University of Beirut and co-founder of the Beirut Urban Lab, a regional research center advancing more inclusive, just, and viable cities. Fawaz's research focuses on urban justice, examining informality, law, land, housing, property, public space, and in-disaster recovery with the aim of informing planning theory and practice. A vocal advocate for the right to housing, inclusive public space, and just urban governance, she publishes across academic and public platforms and has advised on urban and regional development, housing, land, and property. Fawaz has held teaching appointments, honorary professorships, and fellowships in Europe and the U.S. She currently serves as editor for the International Journal of Urban and Regional Research, along with being a member of Planning Theory's editorial board. She also serves on the board of several research and planning bodies in Lebanon and its region. This lecture is part of the Department of City & Regional Planning's fall lecture series.

events.title: Performing Enlightenment: Buddhism and Theater in Early Modern China | Lecture by Mengxiao Wang
events.description: In late Ming and early Qing China, a major revival of Buddhism coincided with a growing fascination with theater. In Performing Enlightenment, Mengxiao Wang examines how Chinese Buddhist monastics and laypeople actively engaged with and transformed the dramatic arts. Drawing on a wide range of religious and literary sources, the book argues that Buddhist practitioners reconciled the tension between spiritual cultivation and worldly entertainment by reimagining theater as a creative mode of devotion. In this process, playwriting, stage performance, and theatergoing all emerged as legitimate pathways to enlightenment. Speaker Bio:Mengxiao Wang is Assistant Professor of Chinese Literature in the Department of East Asian Languages and Cultures at the University of Southern California. She received her Ph.D. from Yale University and was the Sheng Yen Postdoctoral Fellow in Chinese Buddhism at UC Berkeley. Her research explores the intersections of literature and Buddhism in early modern China, with particular attention to theater, ritual, gender, and book history. Her first monograph, Performing Enlightenment: Buddhism and Theater in Early Modern China, was published by the Harvard University Asia Center in 2026. This event is co-sponsored by the Numata Center for Buddhist Studies.

events.title: Seminar 242, Econometrics Seminar: Federico Crippa (University of California, Berkeley) - Manipulation Testing in Boundary Discontinuity Design
events.description: Abstract:We propose the first manipulation test designed for boundarydiscontinuity designs (BDDs) with general boundary shapes. A BDD is amultidimensional extension of the regression discontinuity design (RDD)in which treatment assignment is determined by whether themultidimensional running variable crosses a lower-dimensional boundaryset. The test avoids multivariate density estimation and builds on theobservation that, in the absence of manipulation, observations near theboundary should be approximately evenly split between treatment andcontrol within arbitrary groups defined by their projections onto theboundary. We test this implication using a collection of binomialbalance tests on observations near the boundary, with groups formed byk-means clustering. We establish the asymptotic validity of the testunder suitable regularity conditions. We also evaluate finite-sampleperformance through Monte Carlo simulations and illustrate the test inthree empirical applications.

events.title: What is private equity?
events.description: With Charlie Eaton, Associate Professor of Sociology, UC Merced Private equity investment funds command increasing wealth and reach in the U.S. economy, yet the scope and role of PE remain ambiguous. A new working paper from Charlie Eaton, Albina Gibadullina, Marie-Lou Laprise, and Adam Goldstein assembles systematic data to provide a descriptive anatomy of PE's shifting strategies and ownership patterns in the U.S. since the 1980s. In this talk, Eaton will present the authors' theory of PE through an analysis of four interconnected roles — "corporate raider," "main street invader," "shadow owner," and "monopoly-builder" �� and the changing balance among them over time. He'll show that the industry's traditional role has been replaced with corporate raiders that specialize in restructuring publicly traded firms. Today's PE investors increasingly focus on agglomeration and rationalization of already private "main street" companies. PE-owned companies also increasingly stay private through longer hold times and sales to other PE funds. Ultimately, PE's expansion has helped spread the logic of shareholder value maximization to ever-more corners of the economy, but without the relative transparency and regulation of publicly traded companies.Register Now About the speaker Charlie Eaton is an economic sociologist and associate professor at the University of California, Merced. He investigates the power of elites in politics and the economy, as well as policy and organizational strategies to rebalance power and wealth towards ordinary people. His book, Bankers in the Ivory Tower (University of Chicago Press, 2022), is about the relationship between financialization, student debt, inequalities in higher education, and the rise of financiers among U.S. billionaires. The book won the Pierre Bourdieu Best Book Award from the American Sociological Association. In his latest research, Eaton examines how billionaires from finance and from big tech adopted more oligarchical roles in U.S. politics. The project experiments with machine learning methods for assembling data on billionaire social networks. Eaton writes about this research in his Substack newsletter, "Axis of Oligarchy." Eaton's writing and research have been featured in the New York Times, Washington Post, LA Times, Wall Street Journal, New York Review of Books, Los Angeles Review of Books, Marketplace, CBS, CNN, and PBS. His academic research has been published in journals across the social sciences, including American Sociological Review, Review of Financial Studies, Social Forces, Socio-Economic Review, Sociology of Education, Politics & Society, P.S. Political Science and Politics, Research in Higher Education, Sociological Compass, and Socius.

events.title: Mathematics Department Colloquium: Why I am optimistic about the future of mathematics
events.description: Speaker: Martin Olsson, UC BerkeleyThis is a talk about the cultural and practical aspects of mathematics. Over the last many months I have had nearly daily conversations about AI and math, in a wide variety of settings. On the one hand, I am optimistic about the future of our subject and the profession. At the same time, I am quite concerned about the atmosphere among younger mathematicians, and the public view of the mathematics profession. In this talk I will explain some of the reasons for my optimism, and discuss some concrete suggestions, aimed mostly at younger mathematicians, for navigating this moment. This is not a talk about predicting the future, but instead about how to approach our work without doing so.The views and opinions in this talk are solely my own, and do not reflect the official position or policy of the department or university.

events.title: A Poet in Search of Time: O Changhwan in Moscow
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Janet Poole (University of Toronto) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: Modernist poet O Changhwan left one of the most voluminous literary records of the interregnum—that period marked by the collapse of the Japanese Empire in 1945, dual occupations, and the eruption of civil war in the late 1940s. In such an eventful era, it is perhaps not surprising that survival was on O's mind: survival as a poet, as an aspiring socialist, as a living being. My talk begins and ends with O's poetic travelogue of his 1949 journey to Moscow for medical treatment, but I understand that journey to have begun with his earlier decision to cross the 38th parallel and move to the northern zone of the Korean Peninsula in 1947. In reading O's poems, translations and essays from the interregnum, I hope to write a more provisional history of an early Cold War modernism, one shaped by decolonization and the refusal of anticommunism, and one that sought a home, however transiently, in the nascent revolutionary-socialist state of North Korea. Speaker Bio: Janet Poole teaches in the fields of Korean literature and literary translation at the University of Toronto. Her most recent book Patterns of the Heart and Other Stories (Columbia University Press, 2024) presents an introduction to the little known modernist writer Ch'oe Myŏngik (1903-?). Born and based in Pyongyang throughout his career, Ch'oe's work lovingly details life in that city and chronicles the hopes and dreams for a new society in the age of decolonization. A dedicated literary translator, Poole has also translated works by mid-twentieth century writer Yi T'aejun (1904-?), publishing a collection of his anecdotal essays (Eastern Sentiments) and a selection of his short stories (Dust and Other Stories). A new book project, "Decolonizing Style: Going North and the History of Korean Modernism," looks at the writings of Korea's modernist writers and artists who crossed the 38th parallel into what was to become the Democratic People's Republic in the late 1940s. The project follows upon an earlier study of modernist responses to the fascist regime of the late colonial era, When the Future Disappears: The Modernist Imagination in Late Colonial Korea (Columbia University Press, 2014).

events.title: Michael Roth in Conversation
events.description: Should universities remain institutionally neutral on the great political and social questions of our time? Or does neutrality itself represent a choice about the role universities should play in public life? Michael Roth, president of Wesleyan University, discusses institutional neutrality, academic freedom, and the responsibilities of university leaders in a deeply polarized political environment. Drawing on his experience leading Wesleyan University and his extensive scholarship on higher education, Roth explores when universities should speak, when they should listen, and how institutions can protect open inquiry while engaging the challenges facing democracy. Roth has served as president of Wesleyan University since 2007. A historian, author, curator, and public advocate for liberal education, he previously served as president of California College of the Arts and as associate director of the Getty Research Institute. His books include Safe Enough Spaces: A Pragmatist's Approach to Inclusion, Free Speech, and Political Correctness (2019). Roth visits campus in conjunction with the Townsend Center's yearlong Sawyer Seminar on Neutrality: The Problems and Challenges of the Public University, funded by the Mellon Foundation. He is in conversation with Seminar leaders Stephen Best (English; Townsend Center) and Colleen Lye (English).

events.description: Speaker: Janet Poole (University of Toronto) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: COMING SOON Speaker Bio: Janet Poole teaches in the fields of Korean literature and literary translation at the University of Toronto. Her most recent book Patterns of the Heart and Other Stories (Columbia University Press, 2024) presents an introduction to the little known modernist writer Ch'oe Myŏngik (1903-?). Born and based in Pyongyang throughout his career, Ch'oe's work lovingly details life in that city and chronicles the hopes and dreams for a new society in the age of decolonization. A dedicated literary translator, Poole has also translated works by mid-twentieth century writer Yi T'aejun (1904-?), publishing a collection of his anecdotal essays (Eastern Sentiments) and a selection of his short stories (Dust and Other Stories). A new book project, "Decolonizing Style: Going North and the History of Korean Modernism," looks at the writings of Korea's modernist writers and artists who crossed the 38th parallel into what was to become the Democratic People's Republic in the late 1940s. The project follows upon an earlier study of modernist responses to the fascist regime of the late colonial era, When the Future Disappears: The Modernist Imagination in Late Colonial Korea (Columbia University Press, 2014).

events.title: Naeem Mohaiemen | Celluloid Frontiers: A Missing Can of Film and Stop Genocide
events.description: In conjunction with the exhibition Private Frontiers (https://bampfa.org/program/campus-collaborations-private-frontiers-media-legacies-cold-war), BAMPFA presents A Missing Can of Film (2025), a 44-minute essay film by artist and filmmaker Naeem Mohaiemen. Commissioned by the EVA International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, the project explores the legacy of slain Bangladeshi filmmaker Zahir Raihan and the unresolved complexities of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War The screening will include a conversation between Naeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) and Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator at BAMPFA. Opening remarks by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies and Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATE: Thu, Oct 29, 2026 TIME: 7-8 pm PST VENUE: BAMPFA TICKETS: Tickets for BAMPFA members are now on sale.Tickets for the general public go on sale Friday, August 7 at 11 AM. Buy tickets HERE (https://secure.bampfa.org/33280/33347?_gl=1*ev5un9*_ga*NzQxNDczMzYzLjE3ODU5NjA0MTU.*_ga_SDH80YD3Z1*czE3ODU5NjA0MTUkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODU5NjA5OTAkajYwJGwwJGgw) —About the Film Commissioned by EVA Ireland International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, AMissing Can of Film (2025) traces the lost-left politics buried within Zahir Raihan's Stop Genocide (1971)—a film edited in the style of Soviet Realism and Third Cinema during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War. Raihan, a novelist and director, was abducted only forty-five days after the end of the war. A Missing Can of Film combines scenes from Stop Genocide with footage shot at the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation after the nation's 2024 July Student "Monsoon" Uprising, interrogating the film canister as a vessel of contested history.About the Artist/FilmmakerNaeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) imagines rhizomatic families, malleable borders, and socialist utopias– beginning from postcolonial markers and then radiating outward to unlikely transnational alliances. In spite of underscoring a tendency toward misrecognition of allies, the hope of a future global left, against current categories of race, religion and nation, drives the work. He is author of Prisoners of Shothik Itihash (Kunsthalle Basel, 2014); editor of Chittagong Hill Tracts in the Blind Spot of Bangladesh Nationalism (Drishtipat, 2010); and co-editor w/ Lorenzo Fusi of System Error: War is a Force that Gives us Meaning (Sylvana, 2007).About the DiscussantTausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor) is Assistant Curator at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, where he helped organize the exhibition To Exalt the Ephemeral: The (Im)Permanent Collection. He previously worked as the Spiegel-Wilks Curatorial Fellow at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania and at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Noor's writing, for which he has received awards from the Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant and the Robert B. Silvers Foundation, has been published in various periodicals and journals, including the New Yorker, the New York Times, the New York Review of Books, Art History, and Artforum, as well as in various artist catalogues and edited volumes. He holds degrees from Dartmouth College and Goldsmiths, University of London and is a PhD candidate in History of Art at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: America at 250: Reimagining Who We Are
events.description: Co-hosted by Goldman School of Public Policy, Berkeley Journalism, Berkeley Law, and the Othering and Belonging Institute. As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, UC Berkeley invites the campus and the broader community to reflect on a defining question: What vision will guide America's next 250 years? For two and a half centuries, the United States has been shaped by the aspirations of its founding and by continual debates over identity, belonging, rights, responsibilities, and democratic ideals. Yet many of the institutions that define public life were created for a very different country—demographically, economically, technologically, and culturally. Bringing together students, scholars, innovators, journalists, and civic leaders, America at 250 will explore how the United States can renew its democratic promise and foster a stronger sense of belonging and common purpose in an increasingly diverse and interconnected society. Rather than simply commemorating the past, the summit looks ahead: How can we build and sustain a country that truly secures life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness for all—and how can each of us help shape the next chapter of the American experiment?

events.title: Learning and Pricing for Consumer Electronics Trade-in Program (Sean Zhou, The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
events.location: 1174 Etcheverry Hall, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA
events.description: Title: Learning and Pricing for Consumer Electronics Trade-in ProgramAbstract: We consider a dynamic pricing problem for a two-sided consumer electronics trade-in program, where a firm acquires and re-sells multiple types of pre-owned (used) products over a finite selling horizon. There are customers trading in their used products for new products at discounted prices and customers buying refurbished products. The firm sets trade-in prices and resale prices to maximize its total expected profit. We first consider the scenario where the firm knows the choice models of customers. We design a dynamic policy called the Batched-Adjustment Control (BAC) policy, under which the selling horizon is divided into different consecutive and disjoint batches for different products and the prices in one batch are updated based on the realized uncertainties in the previous batch. We show the profit loss of BAC relative to the optimal profit is in the order of Õ(T¹⁄³). When the firm does not know the choice model parameters of customers, we adopt the framework of exploration-then-exploitation to develop an algorithm called Batched Re-optimization Learning Control (BRLC), in which the firm first uses Maximum Likelihood Estimation to learn the trade-in and demand models' parameters, and then re-optimizes the trade-in and resale prices at the beginning of each batch based on the estimated parameters and realized uncertainties from the preceding batch. We show that BRLC has a regret in the order of O(T¹⁄²), matching the Ω(T¹⁄²) lower bound for general adaptive learning policies. The developed algorithms are very efficient and easy to implement, which can be scaled up for practical problems with a large number of products. This is based on joint works with Zhuoluo Zhang (Xiamen University), Murray Lei (Queens University), and Wenhao Li (SUFE).Bio: Sean Zhou is Professor of Department of Decisions, Operations and Technology, CUHK Business School, and Professor in Department of Systems Engineering and Engineering Management (by courtesy), at The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK). He currently serves as the Associate Dean (research and impact) of CUHK Business School. He has held visiting positions at National University of Singapore and University of Toronto. He received his Ph.D. in Operations Research from North Carolina State University. His main research interests are inventory management, pricing, sustainable operations, data-driven supply chain optimization, and operations and marketing interface. He serves as Area Editor (Inventory and Supply Chain Optimization) of OR Letters, Senior Editor of POMS, and Associate Editor of various journals including Naval Research Logistics and Service Science.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Tania Roy, Duke University | Co-Designing Emerging Devices, Circuits, and Architectures for Edge AI
events.description: Abstract: AI is moving to the edge, where energy, latency, and privacy constraints are the tightest. In conventional von Neumann hardware, data movement rather than computation dominates energy and latency. This talk presents our group's memory-centric co-design work, spanning devices, circuits, and architectures, from the sensor to the memory. First, we compute inside the sensor. Electrically reconfigurable floating-gate optoelectronic synaptic pixels combine light sensing, nonvolatile weight storage, and multiply-accumulate in a single device, so features are extracted where the image is captured. Second, we map transformer attention onto Flash-based content-addressable memory (FlashCAM). Amorphous oxide semiconductor (AOS) Flash devices integrated into 16×16 arrays encode similarity scores directly in their matchline discharge. Third, we present CMOS-compatible non-filamentary memristors for BEOL monolithic 3D integration. They switch at 100 ns with low variation, which allows verification-free, O(1) outer-product programming in 32×32 crossbars. Combined with compact models and BF16-emulating macro architectures, they enable in-situ LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs on the device. Finally, we examine AOS transistor reliability, which is critical for their use as DRAM access transistors in dense, low-leakage GPU memories. We are at an inflection point. AI demand is outpacing silicon scaling, and incremental improvements to CMOS alone will not close the gap at the edge. Emerging hardware deserves a real chance, with circuits and architectures designed around its strengths and non-idealities rather than forcing it to imitate the old devices. This talk invites the device, circuit, and systems communities to build that future together. Bio: Dr. Tania Roy is an Associate Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Duke University, where her group co-designs emerging devices, circuits, and architectures for edge AI hardware. Her work spans in-sensor computing with optoelectronic synapses, in-memory computing with oxide-semiconductor Flash and non-filamentary memristors, and the reliability and radiation effects of amorphous oxide semiconductors and GaN. She is the co-founder of Synapse Semiconductor, a startup commercializing her group's research. Before joining Duke in 2023, she was a faculty at the University of Central Florida from 2016 to 2022. Before that, she was a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley from 2014 to 2016 and at Georgia Tech from 2012 to 2013. She received the PECASE in 2024, Duke's Langford Lecture Award in 2025, and the NSF CAREER Award in 2019. She has served as General Chair of the Device Research Conference and as Chair of the IEDM Emerging Device and Compute Technology subcommittee. She received her MS and PhD in Electrical Engineering from Vanderbilt University.

events.title: David Brandman: Human Intracortical brain-computer interfaces and translational neurotechnology
events.description: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) record neural activity and decode it in real time, giving people with paralysis a way to control external devices or communicate. They also offer a rare window into how the human brain represents complex behavior at the level of individual neurons. In this talk, I will present results from the ongoing BrainGate2 clinical trial, in which participants with paralysis have microelectrode arrays implanted in speech-related areas of the ventral precentral gyrus. I will describe how neural populations in this region encode attempted speech, and how decoding these signals allowed a man with ALS to communicate with 99% word accuracy across a 125,000-word vocabulary. I will then discuss our brain-to-voice work, which shows that the same cortical activity carries not only phonemic content but also paralinguistic features such as intonation, and which now consistently yields intelligible offline speech reconstruction. Finally, I will discuss how clinical neurosurgery creates opportunities for first-in-human discoveries about brain function, and highlight ongoing clinical trials developing restorative neurotechnologies for people living with paralysis.

events.title: Group Actions and Dynamics Seminar: Local statistics of the Laplace spectrum on 3D rectangular flat tori
events.description: Speaker: Wooyeon Kim, KIASIn this talk, we show that the pair correlation of the Laplacian eigenvalues on 3-dimensional rectangular flat tori follows Poissonian statistics. Similar to the earlier work of Eskin, Margulis, and Mozes on 2D flat tori, these eigenvalues are represented by values of positive definite quadratic forms at integer points. In the 3D case, the problem reduces to a special case of the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for rapidly shrinking intervals. Our approach reformulates the problem in terms of homogeneous dynamics via theta functions on $(SL_2(R)/SL_2(Z))^3$, and relies on a quantitative estimate for escape of mass in this space. This is joint work with Jens Marklof and Matthew Welsh.

events.description: Epic yet intimate, sweeping yet personal, La maison des bois stands as one of the greatest achievements in the history of television, as well as legendary director Maurice Pialat's magnum opus. events.title: Claudio Lomnitz | "Antropología de la Zona de Silencio" (Anthropology in the Zone of Silence)
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event Description What does it mean to live in a place where violence has made speaking dangerous? The Politics in Private Working Group invites you to a public lecture and conversation with anthropologist Claudio Lomnitz, who will speak about his book Antropología de la Zona de Silencio (ERA 2025). Focusing on Zacatecas, Lomnitz's book examines how the struggle among criminal groups has transformed municipalities, urban neighborhoods, ranches, and borders, producing new forms of economic and social control through extortion, manipulation, and fear. Please note that we will meet in person, and Dr. Lomnitz will join remotely through Zoom. The book takes the "zone of silence" as a starting point for understanding how violence reshapes the social and political landscape. In these regions, conventional forms of communication and reporting become increasingly constrained, while rumor and other informal channels become essential ways of navigating everyday life. Lomnitz's account also follows the devastating consequences of this transformation, from forced disappearances and the destruction of local communities to the emergence of spaces for training and recruiting armed groups. Join us for this remote lecture and conversation on violence, silence, organized crime, and the changing social landscape of contemporary Mexico. All are welcome.Organized by the Politics in Private Working Group, supported by CLACS.SpeakerClaudio Lomnitz is Campbell Family Professor of Anthropology at Columbia University and a member of El Colegio Nacional. His scholarship brings together anthropology, history, and political theory to examine Mexican society, with particular attention to nationalism, political culture, the state, violence, and the formation of modern Mexico. He is the author of numerous works, including Exits from the Labyrinth: Culture and Ideology in the Mexican National Space, Death and the Idea of Mexico, and The Return of Comrade Ricardo Flores Magón (he spoke (https://clacs.berkeley.edu/return-comrade-ricardo-flores-magon) and wrote (https://clacs.berkeley.edu/mexico-geography-ideology-and-revolution) about it with CLACS in 2014). His recent work turns to the anthropology of violence and the social worlds produced in its wake, including his books Sovereignty and Extortion (Duke, 2024) and Antropología de la Zona de Silencio (ERA, 2025).

events.title: Bergman Lecture in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Karen Goldberg, Vagelos Professor of Energy Research, University of PennsylvaniaOrganometallic Complexes and Molecular Oxygen: Developing Mechanistic UnderstandingMolecular oxygen represents the ideal oxidant to use in chemical oxidations. It is abundantly available, inexpensive (particularly if used without separation from air) and environmentally benign. However, in homogeneous metal-catalyzed organic oxidations, more expensive and/or hazardous oxidants are often employed. A limiting factor in the development of homogeneous catalytic systems for aerobic oxidations has been a lack of mechanistic understanding of exactly how transition metal complexes react with molecular oxygen. Traditionally, organometallic chemists rigorously protect their compounds from oxygen and so our knowledge of the reactivity of organometallic compounds and oxygen is severely underdeveloped. In this presentation, kinetic and mechanistic studies of the reactions of molecular oxygen with several late metal complexes will be presented along with our nascent understanding of the various mechanistic pathways available for oxygen insertion reactions. The opportunities and potential for the incorporation of such reactions into hydrocarbon functionalization strategies will also be discussed.

events.title: Globally Converging Algorithm for Multistage Stochastic Mixed-Integer Programs Via Enhanced Lagrangian Cuts (Haoxiang Yang, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen)
events.location: 1174 Etcheverry Hall, UC Berkeley, Berkeley, CA
events.description: Title: Globally Converging Algorithm for Multistage Stochastic Mixed-Integer Programs Via Enhanced Lagrangian CutsAbstract: This work proposes a globally converging cutting-plane algorithm for solving multistage stochastic mixed-integer programs with general mixed-integer state variables. We demonstrate the generation process of Lagrangian cuts and show that Lagrangian cuts capture the convex envelope of value functions on a restricted region. To approximate nonconvex value functions to exactness, we propose to iteratively add binary state variables and generate Lagrangian cuts on the lifted state space. This lift-and-cut procedure converges to the global optimum with probability one. We further propose two types of enhanced Lagrangian cuts, Pareto-optimal Lagrangian cuts and square minimization cuts, to improve the computational performance of vanilla Lagrangian cuts. Extensive computational experiments on the generation expansion planning and stochastic unit commitment problems demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed methodology in solving large-scale, multistage stochastic mixed-integer programs.Bio: Haoxiang Yang is an assistant professor at the School of Data Science, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-SZ). He graduated with a PhD degree from the Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences at Northwestern University in 2019. Prior to joining CUHK-SZ, he worked in Los Alamos National Laboratory between 2019 and 2021 as a postdoctoral research associate. Haoxiang's research focuses on the theory of optimization under uncertainty, specifically in stochastic programming and robust optimization, integer programming and nonlinear programming, with its applications in energy systems, supply chain and logistics, disaster relief and sports analytics. Haoxiang serves on the Committee on Stochastic Programming (COSP), the governing board of the Stochastic Programming Society.

events.title: Logic Colloquium: 1Gödel's Footnote'
events.description: Speaker: Stephen Mackereth, University of Notre DameGödel intended his Dialectica translation to provide a reduction of first-order arithmetic to a quantifier-free theory T. It has widely been objected that this theory T tacitly presupposes the very quantificational logic that Gödel was trying to eliminate, hidden within its complicated definition of "computable function of finite type." This would render the translation philosophically circular. Gödel was adamant that there was no circularity here, but so far an explicit analysis has been wanting. I defend G��del, showing that there is no circularity and answering a longstanding exegetical question in Gödel scholarship. The foundations of Gödel's theory T are stranger than meets the eye; they utilize a Leibnizian notion of analyticity in a surprising way.

events.description: The Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) presents workshop performances of Under Light, a student-led dance workshop choreographed by Naomi Qianxun Lyu.Showtimes:October 29th at 7:00pm (https://events.berkeley.edu/TDPS/event/323316-fall-workshop-performance-under-light-by-naomi-lyu)October 29th at 8:30pm (https://events.berkeley.edu/TDPS/event/334913-fall-workshop-performance-under-light-by-naomi-lyu)October 30th at 7:00pm (https://events.berkeley.edu/TDPS/event/334956-fall-workshop-performance-under-light-by-naomi-lyu)October 30th at 8:30pm (https://events.berkeley.edu/TDPS/event/334957-fall-workshop-performance-under-light-by-naomi-lyu)About the Show: This work examines how systems construct visibility and shape action, asking what it means to move within structures that determine who is seen, positioned, or valued. Drawing on the logic of chess, the piece frames performers as both agents and instruments, appearing to act while being shaped by a larger system. It asks what it means to be visible when movement is already scripted, and what kind of agency is possible within conditions one does not control. events.title: Film Screening: A Woman is a Woman
events.description: Jean-Luc Godard's third feature was conceived "within the framework of a neorealist musical," with nods to René Clair and Ernst Lubitsch. Anna Karina is Angela, an occasional stripper in a shabby club called the Zodiac. She is determined to have a baby and soon; when her lover Emile (Jean-Claude Brialy) won't, she turns to his friend Alfred Lubitsch (Jean-Paul Belmondo), who will. There is magic in this film, from actual hat tricks to the famous egg-frying gag to the mesmerizing traveling shots. Godard's sense of woman as mystery is a part of that magic. (Even the title throws up its hands.)

events.title: Film Screening: Vivre sa vie
events.description: Vivre sa vie depicts Nana (Anna Karina), a naive shopgirl, at the brief, flickering moment when she takes responsibility for her life. Nana takes to the streets, becoming a prostitute and a student of human emotions. Brechtian in its use of twelve dispassionately announced tableaux, Vivre sa vie is also intensely personal. Nana's crucible is Jean-Luc Godard's existential epiphany: Nana struggles to see, and say, things as they are, bravely concluding, "All is good." In the famous scene in a movie theater, Nana's rapt attention to Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc is a tribute to another who sacrificed control to take control.

events.description: Breathtakingly photographed on hand-painted sets, Kwaidan is at once a Japanese woodcut writ large, and an abstract wash of luminescent colors that seem to come from another world. All are tales of mortals caught by forces beyond their comprehension when the supernatural world intervenes in their lives. This version of Kwaidan is the original three-hour Director's Cut.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Fermionic optimal transport
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Paola Zurlo, Universita degli Studi Aldo Moro, Bari, ItalyWe consider optimal transport between quantum dynamical systems on $Z_2$ graded von Neumann algebras. In the usual, non-graded setting , Wassersrein distances between quantum systems can be defined in terms of transport plans of tensor products involving the commutant of one of the algebras. We briefly recall this construction and describe its extension to the graded setting, where the usual commutant and tensor product are replaced by the twisted commutant and the Fermi tensor product. The main point of the construction is a correspondence between fermionic and usual transport plans. More precisely, using cyclic representations associated with transport plans and the Klein isomorphisms induced by the gradings, we establish a one-to-one correspondencebetween fermionic transport plans and graded transport plans in the usual tensor product. This correspondence allows the Wasserstein distances in the fermionic setting to be related to the corresponding distances in the non-graded setting, and in particular yields their metric properties.

events.title: NORTH STAR: A Movement Workshop
events.description: "you begin underneath all that concrete, down inside corridors, labyrinthine" —Quincy Troupe, "moving toward the open, toward the light" About the workshop: Where are you; where am I? How do we orient ourselves in relation to one another? In dialogue with the children's game "Marco Polo"—in which players with closed eyes orient themselves in response to sound and voice—artist Steffani Jemison will lead participants through a series of playful prompts connecting perspective, movement, language, and relation through guided improvisation. Gameplay will be preceded by a somatic warm-up and will integrate theory, fiction, and poetry; references may include Dionne Brand and Tyrone S. Palmer alongside Quincy Troupe. The workshop is suitable for anyone interested in testing contact, entanglement, and antagonism through lived experience; it might resonate particularly with creative writers, theorists, and performing artists. Physical movement in this workshop is adaptable to all bodies and physical capacities; no movement experience required. Come as you are.About the Artist: Steffani Jemison is an interdisciplinary artist and writer. In dialogue with interlocutors (living and ancestral), her work connects mark-making, gesture, projection, movement, and document. In 2026, her work is included in solo and group exhibitions at Lafayette Anticipations, Paris, FR; the New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York, NY; the Westfälischer Kunstverein, Münster, DE; the Moody Center, Houston, TX; the Studio Museum in Harlem, New York, NY; Buffalo AKG, Buffalo, NY; and the Carpenter Center, Cambridge, MA; among other venues. Jemison's work is part of many public collections, including the Museum of Modern Art, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Guggenheim Museum, the Stedelijk Museum, and the Studio Museum in Harlem. Jemison's novella A Rock, A River, A Street was published by Primary Information in 2022. She is an Associate Professor in the Department of Art & Design at Rutgers University-New Brunswick.

events.title: TAC Seminar - Konstantinos Kritos (Johns Hopkins)
events.description: Title: Two in one: gravitational-wave and electromagnetic signals from dense stellar environmentsAbstract: The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaborations have observed a plethora of stellar-mass binary black holes merging in the local Universe through the detection of gravitational waves. Simultaneously, the JWST has revealed a diverse population of supermassive black holes and bound star clusters within the first billion years after the Big Bang. Moreover, an abundant number of Little Red Dots, which are hypothesized to be a new class of actively accreting massive black holes, have also been discovered by the JWST at high redshifts. In this seminar, I will introduce RAPSTER, a population synthesis code that simulates the evolution of the million-body problem within seconds, and is used to generate catalogs of compact object coalescences and stellar disruption events by compact objects in star clusters. I will argue that dense star clusters are ideal environments for the assembly of intermediate-mass black holes that bridge the gap between the stellar and supermassive species. Moreover, high-energy few-body dynamical interactions involving a massive black hole lead to rich multimessenger signals including extreme-mass ratio inspirals and tidal disruption events, that can be observed by current and future telescopes, such as the Rubin Observatory, the Roman Space Telescope, and LISA.Host: TBD
