events.title: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing
events.description: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing Monday, November 2, 12:30 - 2:00 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1Rd-bqIFW9uq2WJK95uHg8WOYJHOAI14DXYfJCj-d0fk/edit) The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing (Cambridge University Press, 2026) examines the politics of Tunisia after the Arab Spring. Tunisia emerged as the one success story to transition to democracy, winning a Nobel Peace Prize in 2015 for its focus on inclusion and power-sharing. How, then, did its democracy collapse in 2021? Drawing on unique interviews with senior Tunisian officials, alongside three nationally representative surveys of the population, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy points to an overemphasis on compromise, consensus, and power-sharing. Although power-sharing institutions can be useful at the start of a transition, the book finds that extending them beyond that point can lead democracy to unravel by frustrating voters and spurring the rise of populists and extremists. The book takes an in-depth look at Tunisia's transition and then explores how far the theory travels through a quantitative analysis of all democratic transitions between 1942–2020. Overall, the book reveals the dark side of power-sharing, broadening our understanding of the causes of populism, polarization, and democratic breakdown. Sharan Grewal is an Associate Professor of Government at American University (https://www.american.edu/spa/faculty/sgrewal.cfm) and a Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution (https://www.brookings.edu/experts/sharan-grewal/). He was previously assistant professor at William & Mary and a research fellow at the Middle East Initiative (https://www.belfercenter.org/person/sharan-grewal) at Harvard. He received a PhD in Politics from Princeton University in 2018. Sharan's research examines revolutions and democratic transitions, particularly in the Arab world. His first book, Soldiers of Democracy? Military Legacies and the Arab Spring (Oxford University Press, 2023), explores the conditions under which militaries support or thwart democratic transitions, drawing on interviews and surveys of military personnel in Egypt and Tunisia. It received APSA's Best Book in MENA Politics (https://apsamena.org/2024/10/19/2023-mena-politics-section-award-winners/) Award and the Robert Jervis Best International Security Book (https://apsanet.org/membership/organized-sections/organized-section-awards/past-awards/section-19/) Award. His second book, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing, is forthcoming with Cambridge University Press in October 2026. Sharan's work has also been published in the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, and British Journal of Political Science, among other journals. These papers have explored when Islamists become democrats, how discrimination shapes Muslim migrants, and why US training politicizes foreign militaries. These pieces have won Best Paper and Article Awards from APSA MENA and APSA's Democracy & Autocracy section, as well as the Perry World House-Foreign Affairs Emerging Scholars Prize. Sharan's research has received funding from the National Science Foundation, the Henry Luce Foundation, the John Templeton Foundation, the Smith Richardson Foundation, and the Defense Security Cooperation University. He writes regularly about Middle East politics for Brookings andthe Washington Post, and has been interviewed by the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and Reuters, among others. He serves on the editorial board of the journal Comparative Politics.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Chenhao Jin: Emergent Excitations in Semiconducting Moiré Superlattices
events.description: Emergent Excitations in Semiconducting Moiré Superlattices Excitations in quantum systems govern their responses to intrinsic and extrinsic perturbations. Emergent excitations from the interplay between topology and correlation can drive new phase instabilities and enable novel device concepts. While a plethora of intriguing ground states are reported in two-dimensional flatband systems, it has been challenging to directly probe excitations, particularly those decoupled from the charge sector. In this talk, I will discuss our recent efforts to investigate excitations in semiconducting moiré superlattices. We developed an ultrafast imaging technique to record their complete space-time evolution, such as space-and-time-resolved transport. This allows us to simultaneously capture and separate multiple collective excitations, identify their nature, and distinguish them from conventional ones. These emergent excitations govern dynamic responses of the system and play a central role in phase stability and transition. Our results highlight new insights encoded in collective excitations and open avenues for studying and engineering correlated quantum systems through nonequilibrium approaches.Speaker Bio: Dr. Chenhao Jin is an assistant professor of Physics at UC Santa Barbara. He received a B.S. in Physics from Peking University and PhD in Physics from UC Berkeley. He was a Kavli fellow at Cornell University before moving to UC Santa Barbara in 2021. Dr. Jin's research focuses on developing new optical spectroscopy and imaging techniques to "watch" quantum phenomena in space and time; and has made seminal contributions to optical studies of van der Waals materials and moiré superlattices. Dr. Jin has received multiple awards, including AFOSR YIP award, NSF CAREER award, ARO ECP award, Blavatnik Regional Awards for Young Scientists, and Sloan Research Fellowship.

events.title: RTG Arithmetic Geometry, Number Theory and Representation Theory Seminar: Algebraic theory of indefinite theta functions
events.description: Speaker: Kenz Kallal, Princeton UniversityJacobi's theta function $\Theta (q) := 1 + 2q + 2q^4 + 2q^9 + \cdots $, and more generally the theta functions associated to positive-definite quadratic forms, have the property that they are modular forms of half-integral weight. The usual proof of this fact is completely analytic in nature, using the Poisson summation formula. However, Θ is also related to diffusion of heat on a uniform circle-shaped material: it is a restriction of the fundamental solution to the heat equation on a circle. By algebraically characterizing the heat equation as a specific flat connection on a certain bundle on a modular curve, we produce a completely algebraic technique for proving modularity of theta functions. More specifically, we produce a refinement of the algebraic theory of theta functions due to Moret-Bailly, Faltings–Chai, and Candelori. As a consequence of the algebraic nature of our theory and the fact that it applies to indefinite quadratic forms / non-ample line bundles (which the prior algebraic theory does not), we also generalize the Kudla–Millson analytic theory of theta functions for indefinite quadratic forms to the case of torsion coefficients. This is joint work with Akshay Venkatesh.

events.title: Seminar 271, Development: Gabriel Granato - "Can Religion Bridge Ethnic Divides? Pastors, Chiefs, and a Field Experiment on Collective Action"
events.description: Abstract: Ethnic fragmentation is often associated with worse economic development. In one prominent mechanism, free-riding in heterogeneous societies undermines public good provision. This paper examines whether religious and ethnic leaders can sustain cooperation in a voluntary public-works program in an ethnically diverse city in the D.R. Congo. Residents are randomly assigned to ethnically homogeneous or mixed work teams that either include an ethnic chief, a pastor, or no leader at all. Chiefs increase work by 6.0 percentage points in homogeneous teams but not in mixed ones, while pastors increase work by 5.8 points in mixed teams but not in homogeneous ones. Heterogeneity by the strength of ethnic attachment explains this reversal. Chiefs still mobilize their coethnics on mixed teams, and on homogeneous teams their effect is concentrated among teams of residents who report a strong ethnic identity. Pastors do increase work on homogeneous teams whose members have weak ethnic attachments, and their effect is largest on mixed teams whose members hold strong but competing ethnic identities. A cross-randomized public disclosure intervention provides further evidence that the chief mobilizes labor contributions through social enforcement while the pastor uses internal incentives. The paper provides the first experimental evidence on how religious leaders can sustain voluntary public-goods provision in fragmented societies.

events.title: R. Aída Hernández Castillo | Digging for Hope: A Feminist Ethnography in the Land of Mass Graves
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event description In the shadow of Mexico's ongoing human rights crisis, Digging for Hope: A Feminist Ethnography in the Land of Mass Graves (University of Arizona Press, 2026) offers a powerful feminist ethnography of resistance, care, and collective memory. Drawing on nearly a decade of fieldwork, R. Aída Hernández Castillo documents the courageous work of women-led search collectives who, in the face of extreme violence, search for their disappeared loved ones. Through physical and spiritual practices such as exhumation, mourning, and poetic remembrance, these women reclaim dignity for the dead and challenge a society that has normalized disappearance. At the heart of this book is a profound exploration of what Hernández Castillo calls a "pedagogy of love" — a political and ethical framework rooted in care, solidarity, and the refusal to forget. These women are not only searching for bodies; they are building emotional communities, crafting new languages of justice, and offering a reimagining of what it means to resist violence. Their practices, often overlooked by traditional scholarship, restore humanity and dignify the disappeared. Digging for Hope is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand the gendered dimensions of violence and the grassroots movements that rise in response. With clarity and compassion, Hernández Castillo brings readers into the intimate spaces of grief and resistance, offering a model for feminist ethnography that is both rigorous and deeply humane. Hernández Castillo will discuss her book in conversation with Diana Negrin and Omar Gómez Trejo. Hybrid event: in person and on Zoom. Zoom meeting link: https://berkeley.zoom.us/j/99595708560SpeakersRosalva Aída Hernández Castillo is a professor and senior researcher at the Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropología Social (Center for Research and Higher Studies in Social Anthropology) in Mexico City. Her academic work has promoted Indigenous and women's rights in Latin America with a focus on Mexico's incarcerated and disappeared populations. She is the author of 22 books.Diana Negrin (Geography) is a geographer and curator with a focus on identity, space, and social movements in Latin America and the United States. She conducts ethnographic and archival research in the Mexican states of Jalisco and Nayarit with a primary focus on urban Indigenous university students and young professionals. Her scholarship engages human and cultural geography, critical race theory, cultural studies, political ecology and urban studies. Her current research examines the politics of solidarity within interracial and cross-geographic alliances that mobilize around Indigenous culture and territory.Omar Gómez Trejo received his law degree from the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (National Autonomous University of Mexico) and holds a master's from the Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales (Latin American Faculty of Social Sciences). He worked for the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights for 12 years in Mexico and Central America. He was the Executive Secretary of the Interdisciplinary Group of Independent Experts for the Ayotzinapa case (2015-2016) and was the lead Prosecutor of the Special Unit for the Investigation and Litigation of the Ayotzinapa case at Mexico's Attorney General Office from June 2019 to September 2022. Most recently, he was a visiting scholar at the Berkeley Law Human Rights Center through the Practitioners at Risk program.

events.title: Seminar 208, Microeconomic Theory: "Asymmetric Rationality: Protocol Design and Behavioral Anomalies."
events.description: Abstract: We study how asymmetric rationality in strategic interactions can generate seemingly anomalous patterns of belief updating and behavior. A boundedly rational receiver designs a finite-state decision protocol to learn from a fully rational, privately informed, and biased sender who controls the flow of information. The receiver must allocate scarce memory between learning and incentive provision. We identify a simple class of protocols sufficient for optimal design and show how their structure generates information disengagement, indecision, and polarization. The receiver hesitates before deciding but becomes unresponsive to further evidence afterward. Identical receivers following the same protocol can reach opposing decisions despite receiving the same sequence of signals, with the probability of disagreement remaining bounded away from zero as their payoffs approach the optimum. These behaviors, which might otherwise appear erratic or psychologically driven, arise from the strategic use of limited memory.

events.title: Shu-ou Shan: "Accurate Decision Making during Protein Biogenesis"
events.description: Proper protein biogenesis is a pre-requisite for the generation and maintenance of a functional proteome. Accumulating data show that this process begins early, when nascent proteins emerge from the ribosome. Within seconds, the nascent polypeptide must engage the correct set of biogenesis factors and commit to the proper biogenesis pathway. These early decisions profoundly influence the folding, assembly, localization, maturation, and quality control of nascent proteins. How are nascent proteins selected and triaged into the appropriate biogenesis pathways? How does the cellular chaperone network handle aggregation-prone membrane/organellar proteins during their biogenesis? Our work aims to address these fundamental questions at biochemical and biophysical resolution, by integrating quantitative approaches in biochemistry, biophysics and mechanistic enzymology with structural and molecular cell biology. In this talk, I will describe recent work that begin to elucidate how diverse protein biogenesis machinery coordinate in space and time at the ribosome to ensure the efficiency and fidelity of cotranslational protein biogenesis, and how the biophysical properties of nascent proteins shaped the emergence of multi-layered biogenesis pathways.

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Chung-Pei Ma: Gravity's Fatal Attraction: Black Holes at the Centers of Galaxies
events.description: Gravity's Fatal Attraction: Black Holes at the Centers of Galaxies Black holes are spectacular end products of the fatal attraction of gravity. Residing at the centers of galaxies, supermassive black holes have masses up to 20 billion suns and directly impact the evolution of their host galaxies. I will highlight recent progress in studying black holes in the giant elliptical galaxy M87 and other massive galaxies enabled by integral-field spectroscopy on the James Webb Space Telescope and the Keck Telescopes. I will also discuss the implications of these results for the low-frequency gravitational waves from merging supermassive black hole binaries probed by the ongoing Pulsar Timing Array experiments. Speaker Bio: Chung-Pei Ma is the Judy Chandler Webb Professor in Physical Sciences and Distinguished Professor in Astronomy and Physics at UC Berkeley. She uses luminous matter to study dark components in the universe: dark matter, dark energy, and black holes. Her research group develops both theoretical and observational tools to investigate the cosmic assembly of black holes and galaxies. She is an avid violin player and was a student at the New England Conservatory of Music in Boston while pursuing her undergraduate and PhD studies in physics at MIT.

events.title: Julia Budka (LMU Munich), "Cultural Diversity in the Nile Valley during the New Kingdom: Challenging Monolithic Understandings of Egypt and Nubia"
events.description: In recent years, Egyptian and Sudanese archaeology has made significant progress in exploring cultural variability and diversity. Moving beyond oversimplified notions of identity, the concept of cultural diversity enables us to develop more nuanced narratives by integrating a wide range of archaeological evidence and analytical approaches. This lecture offers a fresh perspective on cultural diversity in the Nile Valley during the New Kingdom, drawing on recent excavations and new scientific analyses of material culture. It highlights the complexity of ancient social dynamics and challenges modern perceptions of fixed cultural and political boundaries between Pharaonic Egypt and Nubia (present-day northern Sudan). Furthermore, it questions the long-standing assumption that Egyptian and Nubian societies can be understood as culturally homogeneous or monolithic entities.

events.title: Tendon thread feat. Tanya Lukin Linklater
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture, presented as part of BCNM's Indigenous Technologies program, curated by Indigenous Technologies Coordinator Talia Dixon, co-sponsored by the Arts Practice Department, the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies, and the Graduate Students of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies with Tanya Lukin Linklater Artist-Choreographer and Faculty Mentor, Institute of American Indian Arts - Monday, November 2, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScK01nSupvyyNJV1xSGzG8Gol7h0iXJEiqUM9ucuwBhNkMCuA/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=N3FoYm1uYWs0b25vb2FnazZyaDcybWhxNzYgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Compelled by lineages of Sugpiaq cultural work and their continuance despite imperial and colonial disruptions of their lifeways, Tanya Lukin Linklater will discuss her ongoing practice of visiting ancestral belongings — Sugpiaq technologies — in museum collections, including UC Berkeley's Hearst Museum of Anthropology. The talk will then bring into focus her speculative responses to photographic documentation of Sugpiaq belongings in the Kunstkamera in St. Petersburg, Russia. Coupled with her meditations on estuaries, grasses, and customary practices of the Kodiak archipelago, these threads organize Crested, her solo exhibition at Portikus, Frankfurt, and Tendon thread, a performance commission for the Center for Human Rights and the Arts and Fisher Center at Bard College, premiering in winter 2026. Workshop Opportunity Tanya Lukin Linklater will also host an inclusive workshop for UC Berkeley students and community members that involves creative writing, embodied inquiry, and meditations on Sugpiaq grasses, the following afternoon, Tuesday, November 3, from 4:30 to 6:30 pm, at Bancroft Dance Studio (https://tdps.berkeley.edu/about/directions/bancroft). Participation is limited to 25 people, and registration requires completion of this brief questionnaire (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSf2zl8_3bpc7HPinRsBotpgW9yoCmahdgrUtbY6FTxiMKFRMg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). Participants will be reminded of workshop approximately one week prior. About Tanya Lukin Linklater Tanya Lukin Linklater makes dances in museums, videos, sculptures, and works on paper. She thinks with weather, embodiment, beingness, and ancestral belongings in her practice. She is compelled by scores, orality, poetics, embodied inquiry, Indigenous knowledge transmission, and ephemerality. Her recent and forthcoming exhibitions and performances include Camden Art Centre, London, UK; Dia Art Foundation, New York; National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa; Portikus, Frankfurt; Rudolfinum, Prague; SITE SANTA FE; and Fisher Center at Bard, Annandale-on-Hudson, New York. Her artworks have entered the collections of Agnes Etherington Art Centre, Art Gallery of Ontario, Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Remai Modern, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Tate Americas Foundation, Vancouver Art Gallery, Walker Art Center, and elsewhere. Her book, Slow Scrape (2nd edition, Talonbooks, Vancouver 2022), draws on documentary poetics, concrete-based installations, event scores, and can be read alongside her choreographic practice. Her recent publications include contributions to The Routledge Companion to Indigenous Art Histories in the United States and Canada, Jeffrey Gibson: the space in which to place me, Mark: Sonya Kelliher-Combs, and Native Visual Sovereignty: A Reader on Art and Performance. In 2024 she was awarded a post-doctoral fellowship in Decolonial and Transformational Indigenous Art Practices with Dr. Heather Igloliorte, Canada Excellence Research Chair, at University of Victoria. A dedicated educator, Tanya was a faculty mentor in the Institute of American Indian Arts' MFA in Studio Arts 2021-2026. About Indigenous Technologies Indigenous Technologies is a program of BCNM that engages questions of technology and new media in relation to global structures of indigeneity, settler colonialism, and genocide in the 21st century. Our Indigenous Tech events and ongoing conversations with Indigenous scholars and communities aim to critically envision and reimagine what a more just and sustainable technological future can look like. We highlight Indigenous engagements with robotics, computer science, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, social media, online activism, video games, and more.

events.title: Israel's Post-Election Reckoning: A Conversation with Ilana Dayan
events.description: Inaugural Joan Bieder Journalism Series We are honored to host leading Israeli journalist Ilana Dayan for the inaugural talk in our Joan Bieder Journalism Series. Ilana Dayan is a veteran investigative journalist, anchorwoman, and attorney. She is best known as the long-time host of the investigative television program Uvda (Fact) on the Israeli Channel 12. Ilana Dayan joins us the week following the Israeli elections to discuss, among other things, the election results and what they can tell us about the future direction of Israeli politics, democracy, and society. She will also lend her knowledge and insight to other key issues relating to Israel's domestic, regional, and international concerns. The Helen Diller Institute's annual journalism series is named in memory of Professor of Journalism Joan Bieder, a beloved member of the UC Berkeley faculty and Helen Diller Institute academic community. She passed away in October 2025. Joan Bieder taught at the School of Journalism for 26 years and served as Associate Dean of the J-School for the last eight years of her tenure. She was an active member of the faculty committee of the Helen Diller Institute and an engaged faculty member with the Center for Jewish Studies and The Magnes. events.description: Jim Morken, Professor & Louise and Jim Vanderslice and Family Chair, Boston CollegeMerck Symposium Flyer (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/72-merck-symposium-flyer)Catalytic Stereoselective Synthesis with Boron ReagentsChiral organoboronic esters are versatile intermediates for chemical synthesis. Not only are these compounds stable under a variety of reaction conditions, they are generally non-toxic and can be transformed with minimal generation of hazardous waste. An important feature of aliphatic organoboronic esters is that the boron atom may be replaced with an array of different functional groups through efficient, stereospecific transformations. This seminar will cover new strategies for the construction of alkylboronic esters from simple starting materials in a catalytic enantioselective fashion, and will also discuss ways in which these compounds can functionalized by catalytic stereospecific couplings. In addition, application of organoboronate-based transformations to address compelling problems in chemical synthesis will be discussed. Professor James Morken was born in Concord, California and obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1989 from UC Santa Barbara working with Prof. Bruce Rickborn. He obtained his Ph.D. from Boston College in 1995 with Prof. Amir Hoveyda and was an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with Stuart Schreiber at Harvard University. In 1997, he became an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 2002 and in 2006 joined the faculty of Boston College. In 2014, he was named the Louise and James Vanderslice and Family Chaired Professor of Chemistry at Boston College. Professor Morken's research focuses on the development of transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric processes and their use in complex molecule synthesis. He is particularly interested in the study and development of catalytic enantioselective reactions involving organoboron reagents. Because of the broad array of reactions that available to organoboronates, these types of process can be employed to address a number of compelling problems in the construction of organic frameworks.

events.title: Kapil Ramachandran: Neuroproteasomes and the spatial control of neuronal proteostasis
events.description: Neurons must synthesize proteins at precise times, in response to external cues, and in compartments far from the cell body. Nascent proteins are particularly susceptible to misfolding, yet the mechanisms that rapidly monitor proteins made in dendrites remain poorly understood. We discovered a distinct population of proteasomes that appears to span the neuronal plasma membrane, where these "neuroproteasomes" degrade a subset of proteins during or immediately after translation. Despite evidence for neuroproteasomes across multiple systems, how they associate with the membrane, which proteins they select, and their functions in neurons remain largely unknown. I will argue that neuroproteasomes offer a new cell biological framework for the initiation of protein aggregation, while their constitutive activity converts intracellular proteolysis into extracellular neuromodulation.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics: Joshua Schwartzstein "Channeled Attention and Stable Errors"
events.description: Abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant fail, in the long run, to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn't matter or that a distinction doesn't exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the model. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its stakes; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves. Paper Link: https://gagnon-bartsch.com/files/ChanneledAttention2026.pdf

events.title: Topology Seminar: Exotic R4's with Compactly Supported Diffeomorphisms
events.description: Speaker: Abhishek Shivkumar, UT AustinA diffeomorphism is exotic if it is topologically but not smoothly isotopic to the identity. We show that for diffeomorphisms of closed simply-connected $4$-manifolds dissolving under a single stabilization, there is a natural induced diffeomorphism on an exotic copy of $R^4$. We thereby construct exotic copies of $R^4$ with nontrivial compactly supported mapping class groups of arbitrarily large rank. This follows from a modified construction of corks for exotic diffeomorphisms due to Krushkal-Mukherjee-Powell-Warren. Time permitting, we will show how these examples can be extended to uncountable families thereof by end-summing with a particular exotic R4.

events.title: Harold S. Johnston Lecture
events.description: Steven Brown, Deputy Director, NOAA Chemical Sciences LaboratoryPyrogenic Skies: Photochemistry, heterogeneous chemistry and air quality impacts of wildfire smoke As wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity across North America, their emissions have become a driver of regional air quality degradation. Biomass burning is a large source of ozone precursors, nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), as well as particulate matter that impacts air quality directly and also drives heterogeneous chemical processes. Photochemistry within smoke plumes creates pyrogenic ozone over a variety of timescales, leading to short- and long-range transport and widespread increases in the ozone background. Mixing and entrainment of smoke that is rich in pyrogenic VOCs into NOx-rich urban areas alters regional photochemistry and can further enhance ozone production. However, aerosol loads associated with smoke layers may also suppress photochemistry. Heterogeneous chemistry in smoke plumes influences atmospheric composition through a different set of chemical cycles that affect both the lower and upper atmosphere. A series of recent airborne and ground-based field studies has investigated these chemical processes in biomass burning influenced air. These include the 2019 Fire Influence on Regional to Global Environments and Air Quality (FIREX-AQ), the 2022 California Fire Dynamics Experiment (CalFiDE), the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactivity Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaign, the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone study, and others. These studies provide new insights into the biomass burning influence on tropospheric ozone at all scales, from near field plume chemistry to the global remote troposphere, and from the continental background to local urban influence.

events.title: Fueling Patriarchy: Coal and Gender in the Upper Silesian Cultural Imagination
events.description: As the material foundation of industrialization, coal shaped not only economic processes but also social orders and cultural imaginaries in Central Europe – nowhere more visibly than in Upper Silesia, where coal's materiality helped generate a gendered division of labor: men worked below ground as active providers, women remained above ground in domestic, passive roles. Coal did not merely accompany this patriarchal gender order; it materially produced and sustained it. Drawing on energy humanities and feminist resource theory – most notably Cara Daggett's concept of petromasculinity – this talk traces how this coal-based gender matrix was consolidated, reproduced, and eventually destabilized in Upper Silesian literature, film, and performance from the early twentieth to the twenty-first century. Beginning with early twentieth-century literary representations, I show how cultural production consolidated a patriarchal, heteronormative matrix marked by hypermasculinity and the marginalization of women – a matrix that persisted through socialist realism and postsocialist transformation despite shifting political contexts. Only with the gradual closure of Upper Silesia's coal mines amid Poland's and the Czech Republic's energy transitions in the twenty-first century does a break emerge with this symbolic order: as coal's material grip loosens, so too does the heteronormative order it once underwrote. At the same time, cultural representation takes on a new discursive role, shifting from an instrument consolidating heteronormative codes into a space for renegotiating them. This becomes visible, for instance, in the Netflix series Królowa (2022) and in the drag and burlesque performances of the artistic-research collective Śląsk Przegięty, both of which recast coal and queerness not as opposites but as entangled parts of the region's identity. The talk aims to uncover the entanglements of coal and gender in Upper Silesia, showing how, as coal itself recedes, cultural representation becomes the space where its gender legacies are contested, undone, and reimagined.

events.title: Stefanie Hutka // What Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Stefanie Hutka, design leader and author ofWhat Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation. Stefanie has spent her career asking a question that sounds simple until you try to answer it: what should automation actually do, and for whom? ​Her talk centers on what she calls the "Automation Strategy Gap," the yawning distance between an organization's AI ambitions and its actual readiness to do something useful with them. It is, she argues, alarmingly wide. Drawing on human factors, cognitive science, and management theory, her book makes the case that AI is the latest chapter in a long history of automation, and that the durable lessons were always there, we just got distracted by the hype. One particularly useful provocation: automation accelerates the system you already have. Which means the first thing worth mapping is the beliefs driving your organization before you automate anything at all. ​This is a book launch talk. It will be an essential conversation for anyone who has sat through a roadmap presentation where "AI-powered" was doing a lot of heavy lifting where a strategy should have been. This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Atreyee Gupta
events.description: Atreyee Gupta takes a revelatory look at modernism in India, exploring art's role in decolonization and aesthetic discourse across the Global South. Modernism's peak in the interwar and postwar decades coincided with the eruption of antifascist and decolonization movements globally, including the League against Imperialism, the Bandung Asian-African Conference, and the Non-Aligned Movement. Viewing artistic practices through the lens of the radical intellectual possibilities that these epoch-making events prompted, Atreyee Gupta (History of Art) uncovers a modernist internationalism incongruous with Westernist cultural hegemonies. Modernism, she shows, cannot be separated from concepts of freedom and autonomy generated by Third World political struggles. Gupta mobilizes concepts including liberation, anti-imperialism, development, and modernization as essential analytic categories for art history, reorienting our understanding of both global modernism and Indian art. Intertwining stories of art and liberation, aesthetics and decolonization, and intellectual practices and political revolution in the Third World, or what is now known as the Global South, Non-Aligned (Yale, 2025) follows the far-flung interwar and postwar networks in which Indian artists and intellectuals such as Francis N. Souza, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, and Jagdish Swaminathan participated alongside interlocutors like W. E. B. Du Bois, Richard Wright, Octavio Paz, André Malraux, and Le Corbusier in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

events.title: Italian Lives, Belgian Coal An Environmental History of Labor and Migration
events.description: On June 23, 1946, Italy and Belgium signed the "men in exchange for coal" agreement, in which Italy committed to sending fifty thousand workers each year to the Belgian coal mines, and Belgium pledged to supply a few thousand tons of coal to Italy each month. The first treaty of its kind, the agreement paved the way for the European Coal and Steel Community, a precursor of the European Union. In Italian Lives, Belgian Coal, Daniele Valisena explores the relationship between labor migration, coal extraction, and environmental transformation in the Belgian coalfields of Wallonia. Drawing from French, Italian, and Belgian archival documents; printed primary sources; and oral history interviews conducted by the author, this book breaks new methodological and empirical ground, blending environmental history and the history of migration, historical literature and anthropological work, and history and the contemporary. Each chapter captures and interrogates the agency of different actors, including the Italian and Belgian states, the coal industry, medical experts, miners, and the ecologies that develop in polluted areas left by the coal industry. Italian Lives, Belgian Coal tells a sobering story of the environmental and corporeal injustice wielded by capitalist institutions and its impact on health and medical science, society, and nature.Daniele Valisena, Visiting Fellow, German Historical Institute, UC Berkeley

events.title: Joel Lehman: Open-endedness, Intelligence, and Flourishing
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. events.title: REI Colloquium: Sanctuary Making: Immigrant Families Reshaping Geographies of Deportability
events.location: Social Sciences Building 402 Barrows Hall Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Sanctuary Making: Immigrant Families Reshaping Geographies of Deportability Imigration policy and enforcement practices in the United States now extend beyond the border to the country's interior, impacting the private lives of millions of undocumented and mixed-status families in new ways. Sanctuary Making traces this shift, showing how as enforcement has expanded and deepened, new "hot spots" have appeared across nontraditional sites such as neighborhoods, roads, worksites, hospitals, grocery stores, and homes. Undercurrents of fear, anxiety, and loss permeate the everyday lives of the families navigating these terrains of enforcement. Carolina Valdivia reveals the emotional and material labor of young adults that often underpins families' sanctuary making efforts—strategies to shield against the worst outcomes of enforcement. Many young adults are compelled to take on parental responsibilities and serve as a primary source of emotional support for family members while also brokering legal processes tied to their family's immigration cases. How might policymakers, organizers, educators, and the wider community better support these young people in their efforts to create sanctuary for their families in an increasingly hostile landscape? More about the book: https://www.ucpress.edu/books/sanctuary-making/paper (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/sanctuary-making/paper)This event is co-organized by the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative and the Institute of Governmental Studies' Race, Ethnicity, and Immigration Colloquia Series. The event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Center for Race and Gender.About the Speaker:Carolina Valdivia is an Associate Professor of Criminology, Law and Society at the University of California, Irvine. Carolina's research interests include immigration, law and society, the sociology of education, race and ethnicity, youth and families, and the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Her work explores how various forms of legal and social exclusion impact the lives of immigrant youth and their families, including their educational trajectories, mental health, and political participation. You can find the rest of her biography here: https://carolinavaldivia.org/ (https://carolinavaldivia.org/)This is an accessible event. events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: If it looks like a duck…
events.description: Speaker: Izak Oltman, Northwestern University…and quacks like a duck, it might be a Berezin–Toeplitz operator. In this talk, I will present a version of Beals's theorem for Berezin–Toeplitz operators, specifically for the quantization of the complex projective line. Beals's theorem gives a criterion for recognizing pseudodifferential operators. Roughly speaking, if an operator satisfies certain bounds on its repeated commutators, then it is the quantization of a function with uniform derivative estimates. I will first go over Beals's theorem, then briefly discuss Berezin–Toeplitz operators. Finally, I will present a Beals-type theorem for the complex projective line and go over the proof. The talk will include many animations and examples. This is joint work with Simon Becker and Akshat Kumar.

events.title: Hanna Martens: Aging: A Glitch in the Matrix?
events.description: Aging is accompanied by profound changes in tissue architecture, extracellular matrix (ECM) composition, and mechanical properties. Yet how cells sense and respond to these changes, and how the progressive loss of mechanical homeostasis contributes to age-associated tissue dysfunction, remains poorly understood.Our work explores how mechanotransduction pathways integrate physical cues from the extracellular environment to maintain cellular identity, tissue organization, and organ function throughout life. In particular, we focus on the transcriptional co-regulators YAP and TAZ, key effectors of mechanotransduction that couple ECM-derived signals to gene expression programs governing tissue homeostasis.We investigate how age-associated alterations in YAP/TAZ signaling disrupt the reciprocal relationship between cells and their extracellular environment, promoting cellular senescence, aberrant tissue remodeling, and deterioration of specialized cellular niches. Together, our findings highlight mechanical homeostasis as a fundamental determinant of tissue integrity and suggest that its disruption is an important driver of organ aging and age-associated tissue dysfunction.Division(s): Divisions of Biochemistry, Biophysics & Structural Biology, Division of Cell Biology, Development & Physiology, and Genetics, Genomics, Evolution & Development

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Teacher Organizing Across the Americas: Diverse Strategies for Transforming Unions, Schools, and Society
events.description: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas explores why teachers' unions in Brazil, Mexico, and the United States, representing similar constituencies and fighting for comparable goals, have embraced radically different strategies. Through an ethnographic comparison of teacher organizing in São Paulo, Oaxaca, and New York, the book focuses on three key strategies in teacher organizing—leftist party politics, autonomist politics, and interest group politics—to demonstrate how the strategic choices teachers make matter for both schools and society. In São Paulo, teachers' leftist party politics helped to elect pro-labor presidents five times, with significant social reforms; yet these same politics failed to influence education policy and led to factionalism within the union. In Oaxaca, teachers' autonomous politics led to robust cultural initiatives, an innovative pedagogical proposal, and the capacity to boycott national education reforms. Finally, in many U.S. cities in the 2000s, teachers rejected interest group politics in favor of rank-and-file caucuses that prioritized union-community coalitions and racial justice, which also created new fault lines within the unions and an ambiguous relationship with electoral politics. Teaching Organizing Across the Americas offers important lessons for both scholars and activists interested in transforming institutions like unions to promote more just schools and societies. Rebecca Tarlau is Associate Professor of Education at Stanford University and former Associate Professor of Labor and Employment Relations at Pennsylvania State University, where she was the co-founder of the Consortium for Social Movements and Education Research and Practice. Her ethnographic research focuses on theories of the state and state-society relations; social movements and popular education; Latin American education and development; and labor movements and teachers' work. She is the author of the award-winning Occupying School, Occupying Land: How the Landless Workers Movement Transformed Brazilian Education (OUP, 2019).

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Quantum Interconnects and Modularity via Waveguide QED
events.description: In this talk, we present a demonstration of entanglement distribution via directional photon emission and absorption along a microwave waveguide [1,2]. Superconducting qubits couple to the waveguide at multiple, well-separated locations through modules that deterministically emit and absorb single microwave photons. Using this architecture, we demonstrate directional single-photon emission with 96% fidelity and single-photon absorption exceeding 60% efficiency. We then use partial emission and absorption to generate remote entanglement – a four-qubit W-state ��� between qubits in the emitter and absorber modules with 62% fidelity. Time permitting, we also present an example of driven dissipative entanglement reaching 89% fidelity [3]. These works along with 3D integration target modular and extensible quantum information processing mediated by quantum interconnects. [1] B. Kannan, et al., Nature Physics 19, 394 (2023) | arXiv:2203.01430 (2022) [2] A. Almanakly, et al., Nature Physics 21, 825 (2025) | arXiv:2408.05164 (2024) [3] A. Almanakly, et al., arXiv:2606.13375 (2026) William D. Oliver is jointly appointed the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Professor of Physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he leads the Engineering Quantum Systems Group. He is presently on partial leave as Chief Engineer withGoogle Quantum AI. Will's research interests include the materials growth, fabrication, design, control, and measurement of superconducting qubit processors. From 2003-2023, Will also worked at MIT Lincoln Laboratory – most recently as Laboratory Fellow (2017-2023) – where he was instrumental in growing the quantum computing group to its present levels. Will stepped down from this position to co-found Atlantic Quantum, a quantum computing start-up. Atlantic Quantum was acquired by Google in October 2025. Will is elected Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Fellow of the American Physical Society, and Fellow of the IEEE. He also serves on the U.S. National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee. Will earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University, his M.S. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from MIT, and a B.S. in Electrical Engineering and B.A. in Japanese from the University of Rochester (NY).

events.title: ERG Colloquium Series Fall 2026: Marshall Burke
events.description: Description: Wildfires and the smoke they produce are the fastest growing environmental threat in the US and many other parts of the world. I review recent advances in the measurement of smoke and its constituents, and recent advances in the quantification of both short- and long-term health impacts from smoke exposure and from exposure to the fires themselves. We estimate that short-run smoke exposure causes tens of thousands of deaths annually, a number that will likely grow due to climate change absent substantial intervention. We study the impacts of a leading proposed intervention – prescribed burning – and estimate meaningful net reductions in smoke exposure if the state were to meet its stated prescribed burning targets. Bio: Marshall Burke is professor of Global Environmental Policy in the Doerr School of Sustainability at Stanford, and a senior fellow at the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment, Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, and Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, all at Stanford. He is also a research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. He holds a PhD in Agricultural and Resource Economics from UC Berkeley, and a BA in International Relations from Stanford. He directs the Environmental Change and Human Outcomes Lab at Stanford, is co-founder of AtlasAI, and co-creator of the Environmental Hazards Adaptation Atlas.

events.title: Expecting Inequity: How the Maternal Health Crisis Affects Even the Wealthiest Black Americans
events.description: Racism in maternal healthcare is not reserved for the poor. Wealthier black people are much more likely to die during pregnancy, childbirth, or the postpartum period than their white counterparts. Expecting Inequityfocuses on a San Francisco obstetrics clinic that caters to the affluent, examining the choices around prenatal care and childbirth that class-privileged, pregnant black people are making in order to survive what has been called the "black maternal health crisis."Khiara M. Bridges is the Earl Warren Professor of Public Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. She is a nationally-recognized expert on the intersection of race, class, and reproductive rights. Her scholarship has appeared in the most influential law reviews in the country, including the flagship law journals at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, and UC Berkeley, among many others. She is also the author of several books: Reproducing Race: An Ethnography of Pregnancy as a Site of Racialization (2011), The Poverty of Privacy Rights (2017), and Critical Race Theory: A Primer (2019, 2026). Her fourth book, Expecting Inequity: How the Maternal Health Crisis Affects Even the Wealthiest Black Americans, was released in March 2026. Bridges graduated as valedictorian from Spelman College, receiving her degree in three years. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School and her Ph.D., with distinction, from Columbia University's Department of Anthropology. She speaks fluent Spanish and basic Arabic, and she is a classically-trained ballet dancer who danced professionally in New York City for twenty years before moving to the Bay Area.

events.title: From Evening Fog to Light and Dark: What Sōseki took from "The Tale of Genji"
events.description: Natsume Sōseki is usually read as the Japanese novelist who learned his craft from the West. But what did he take from Murasaki Shikibu, his greatest Japanese predecessor? Although he claimed not to care much for the Tale of Genji, I present evidence in the talk that Sōseki did read the Genji closely. Tracing echoes of the Genji in Sanshiro,The Gate, Kokoro, and Light and Dark, I argue that Sōseki learned more from Lady Muraski than he acknowledged about how the art of the novel can shed light on the darkest corners of the emotional lives of men and women. [BIO] Keith Vincent teaches in the Department of World Languages & Literatures at Boston University, where he directs the MFA Program in Literary Translation. Recent publications include "Genji's Ghosts" in The Literary Imagination (Spring 2026) and "Proust in Japan and Japan in Proust: Notes on Yoshida Jō and the École japonaise of Proust Studies" in Global Japanese History and Culture(Routledge, 2026). Forthcoming this year is an essay on Proust and TheThousand and One Nights.

events.title: [BCLB] Smaller Scope, High Stakes: The EU Due Diligence Directive and Business
events.description: The EU's Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) was once billed as the most ambitious corporate accountability law in the world. It creates a direct obligation on corporations to conduct sustainability and human rights due diligence. Then came the Omnibus. The scope has narrowed and the timeline has shifted, but the directive has not gone away, and it still reaches large non-EU companies with significant business in the EU. What does the CSDDD now require, which U.S. companies remain in scope, and what cannot be negotiated away? Looking ahead, how might further changes to EU rules and diverging U.S. approaches reshape companies' obligations and strategies, and what should businesses be doing now? This BCLB webinar brings together academic, advisory, and law firm perspectives on what the directive means in practice: why it matters for business, how companies are approaching implementation, and whether it makes a real difference for the workers and communities it is meant to protect. Confirmed Speakers: Gustavo Becker, Executive Research Fellow, Berkeley Center for Law and Business Faris Natour, Principal and Co-Founder, Article One Ashley Walter, Partner and Chief Sustainability Officer, Orrick Moderator: Sanchita Banerjee Saxena, Professional faculty member, Haas School of Business and Senior Academic Fellow, Berkeley Center for Law and BusinessRegister here (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_39n2nRyVRN-2KxaKYQ97TQ#/registration)

events.title: Alessandro Ori: From Translation Stalling to Organellar Maps: Molecular Drivers and Therapeutic Targets in Brain Aging and Neurodegeneration
events.description: Aging is the primary risk factor for major neurodegenerative disorders, driven by a progressive breakdown of cellular proteostasis. Yet, uncovering the precise causal mechanisms—and translating them into viable therapeutic strategies—remains a fundamental challenge. In this seminar, I will discuss multi-omics and proteomic advances that illuminate disease drivers across scales, from protein synthesis defects to organellar dysfunction. First, using the turquoise killifish brain aging model, we reveal that protein-transcript decoupling is fueled by ribosome pausing and disome accumulation at basic amino acid stretches (Arg, Lys). This stalling stems from altered tRNA charging, declining building block availability, and molecular ribosome aging, leading to the selective loss of critical RNA-binding proteins like TDP-43. Second, applying cell-type-specific LysoTag proteomics across intact mouse brain lineages, we established a brain lysosome atlas that uncovered cell-tailored organellar functions and novel disease-relevant proteins, notably the neuron-specific glucose transporter SLC45A1 whose loss compromises lysosomal pH and mitochondrial integrity. Furthermore, comparative profiling across neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis models identified a shared lysosomal disease signature centering on sphingolipid catabolism and organelle contact sites. Finally, I will highlight how high-throughput perturb-proteomics in human iPSC-derived neurons couples arrayed CRISPR screening with global proteomic readouts to map TDP-43 loss-of-function phenotypes and accelerate therapeutic target discovery.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: The maintenance of diversity in plant communities: insights from Amazonian forest dynamics and California serptentine annual plants
events.description: Despite centuries of research, many fundamental features of the structure and dynamics of plant communities defy simple explanation. My research group pursues general answers to these questions through integrative approaches that combine community ecology perspectives with insights from functional ecology, floristics and macroecology. Our lab uses a variety of observational, theoretical and experimental approaches, many of them rooted in plant collections and functional trait databases. First, I will share recent projects exploring the dynamics of a large forest plot in the hyperdiverse Ecuadorian Amazon, where we use functional-trait based approaches and novel computational tools to explore the ways in which edaphic specialization, spatial aggregation, and competition dynamics shape one of the most species-rich forests on the planet. Next, I will highlight our recent work in annual plant communities associated with serpentine soils in coastal California, a species-rich system that is ideal for detailed, theoretically-grounded experiments to disentangle mechanisms of species coexistence. Our recent experimental work demonstrates how species trait differences, contrasting responses to spatial and temporal environmental heterogeneity, and complex higher-order interactions combine to shape the diversity of these systems at both local and landscape scales. Finally, I will share insights from my lab's work on continental and global scale patterns of plant diversity, work that is intimately connected to the development of plant trait and occurrence databases. Taken together, these efforts inform our understanding of the mechanisms that drive the fundamental distribution of plant diversity and function across the planet, as well as our predictions of how species and communities will respond to ongoing global change.

events.title: Amogh Dhar Sharma | The Backstage of Democracy: India's Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them
events.description: A talk by Amogh Dhar Sharma (https://www.qeh.ox.ac.uk/people/amogh-sharma), a Leverhulme Early Career Fellow at the University of Oxford, on his new book, The Backstage of Democracy: India's Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/backstage-of-democracy/C063953713758327233B0ACBFF9F37FC), that examines the growing influence of political consultants and data-driven campaigning in Indian elections, revealing how these shifts reflect broader transformations in political expertise, power within parties, and citizen participation. Event moderated by Anahitha Sagar (https://www.linkedin.com/in/anahitha-sagar/) (MPP Candidate' 27) and Arushi Choudhary (https://www.linkedin.com/in/arushi-choudhary-b008ab88/) (MDP Candidate' 27), UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, November 5, 2026 TIME: 3:30-5 pm PST VENUE: 240 Mulford Hall —————- ABOUT THE BOOKOver the last decade, election campaigns in India have undergone a dramatic shift. Political parties increasingly rely on political consultants, spin-doctors, pollsters, and data-driven insights to mobilize voters. But what is driving these changes? Drawing upon my recently published monograph, this talk explores the hidden arena of strategizing and deliberations that takes place between politicians and a new cabal of political professionals as they organize election campaigns in India. I argue that the changes in electioneering are not reducible to a story of technological innovations alone. Rather, they are indicative of a new landscape where ideas of political expertise, the distribution of power within parties, and citizens' attitudes towards political participation have undergone a profound change. ABOUT THE SPEAKERAmogh Dhar Sharma (https://www.qeh.ox.ac.uk/people/amogh-sharma) is a Leverhulme Early Career Fellow in the Oxford Department of International Development, University of Oxford. He holds a PhD from the University of Oxford, where he has previously taught South Asian politics. His first book, The Backstage of Democracy: India's Election Campaigns and the People Who Manage Them, was published by Cambridge University Press in 2024. Currently, he is working on a project on the history of opinion polls and psephology in post-independence India. EVENT POSTER TBD —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Hitchcock Grant Lecture with Kelly Lytle Hernández | Racist by Design - Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control
events.location: Banatao Auditorium, Sutardja Dai Hall - UC Berkeley Campus
events.description: In this lecture, award winning historian Kelly Lytle Hernández will be presenting her work, Racist by Design. She reveals how generations of lawmakers and law enforcers built the American immigration system to encourage white immigrants while targeting nonwhite migrants for exclusion, punishment, and removal. The goal, often explicitly stated by the system's architects, was to create a permanent caste of undocumented and criminalized workers to provide cheap labor for the American economy.About Kelly Lytle Hernández Professor Kelly Lytle Hernández holds The Thomas E. Lifka Endowed Chair in History at UCLA. Her major publications are Migra! A History of the U.S. Border Patrol (University of California Press, 2010), City of Inmates: Conquest, Rebellion, and the Rise of Human Caging in Los Angeles (University of North Carolina Press, 2017), and Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands (W. W. Norton, 2022). Her forthcoming book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control, will be published by W. W. Norton in 2026. In 2016, Professor Lytle Hernández established Million Dollar Hoods (MDH), a university-based but community-driven research initiative that maps the fiscal and human costs of mass incarceration in Los Angeles. She served as the MDH director until 2024 and now serves as the initiative's principal advisor. Professor Lytle Hernández is currently a principal investigator for two additional research collaborations: Mapping Deportations, which maps the history of mass deportation from the United States, and Archiving the Age of Mass Incarceration, which preserves a historic cache of LAPD files and documents the impact of policing on LA residents since the 1970s. For her historical and contemporary work, Professor Lytle Hernández's scholarship has been awarded numerous prizes and honors, including a MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship, and she is currently an elected member of the Society of American Historians, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Pulitzer Prize Board.

events.title: Matrix on Point: Propaganda Machines
events.description: REGISTER Artificial intelligence (AI) is an increasingly powerful force in the current U.S. landscape of knowledge, mis- or disinformation, media, and politics. We are grappling collectively with the ways that AI and associated tech platforms, influencers, and online communities help shape the production of "truths" that drive or ground political energies. At the same time, universities – presumed guardians of critical inquiry and independent knowledge production – are increasingly entering into partnerships with AI companies in a new kind of knowledge compact. This panel brings together scholars who examine questions related to AI, influence, and information in journalism, media, and California's universities to discuss the implications of these developments for information and knowledge politics today. The panel will feature Matyas Bohacek, Researcher at Stanford University; Martha Kenney, Professor of Women & Gender Studies at San Francisco State University; Martha Lincoln, Associate Professor of Anthropology at SF State; and Edward Wasserman, Professor of Journalism at UC Berkeley. Cori Hayden, Director of Social Science Matrix, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS), the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI), the UC Berkeley School of Information, and the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences (EECS).PanelistsMaty Bohacek (https://matybohacek.com/) is a researcher at Stanford University, working at the intersection of AI and media integrity. In a world that is becoming increasingly AI-mediated, his goal is to build AI systems and networks that are inherently trustworthy and interpretable, resulting in productive, democratic discourse. Maty built a deepfake detector for President Zelenskyy of Ukraine and created a deepfake CNN news anchor, which opened a primetime news segment to raise awareness of AI threats. Beyond media integrity, he demonstrated that AI models trained on their own data collapse, developed a method to determine whether specific data were used to train a model, and developed an AI-powered sign language translator. His work has been featured in Forbes, CNN, Science, Nature, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and others.Martha Kenney (https://transforms.sfsu.edu/martha-kenney) is a Professor of Women & Gender Studies at San Francisco State University. She earned a Ph.D. from the History of Consciousness at UC Santa Cruz, where she was a founding member of the Science & Justice Research Center. Located in the tradition of feminist science studies, her research examines how narratives from new fields of biomedical research ��� such as environmental epigenetics and precision medicine—support, contest, and reconfigure collective visions of social justice, environmental justice, and health equity. She has a track record of collaborative, interdisciplinary inquiry, often publishing with colleagues across institutions and national contexts. She was recently a TUM Global Visiting Professor at the Department of Science, Technology, and Society at the Technical University of Munich. She is currently a Health Equity Institute Faculty Scholar at SFSU.Martha Lincoln (https://anthropology.sfsu.edu/people/martha-lincoln) is a medical and cultural anthropologist. Prior to joining the Anthropology Department at SF State in 2017, she received her Ph.D. from the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Prevention Research Center, affiliated with UC Berkeley's School of Public Health. Broadly, her research addresses the cultural politics of public health, biopolitics, and the effects of political economic change on health systems and health outcomes. Since 2008, she has conducted field research in Vietnam, leading to published research on Hanoi's informal sector, stratification and deregulation in health care provision, the ghosts of war, alcohol use and drinking cultures, the redefinition of poverty under late socialism, and urban cholera outbreaks. Her book, Epidemic Politics in Contemporary Vietnam: Public Health and the State, was published in 2021 by Bloomsbury Academic. She serves as co-editor-in-chief of the Journal of Vietnamese Studies. Her current project is based in the United States, and focuses on affective economies in medical crowdfunding for cancer.Edward Wasserman (https://journalism.berkeley.edu/person/ed_wasserman/), Professor of Journalism at UC Berkeley, served as Dean of the Graduate School of Journalism from 2013 to 2020. Before coming to Berkeley, he spent a decade as the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation Professor of Journalism Ethics at Washington and Lee University, home of the nation's first college-level journalism program. Wasserman's journalism career spanned 30 years. He was CEO and editor in chief of American Lawyer Media's Miami-based Daily Business Review newspaper chain, executive business editor of The Miami Herald, city editor of The Casper (Wyo.) Star-Tribune, and editorial director of Primedia's 140-publication Media Central division in New York. Wasserman received a B.A. cum laude in politics and economics from Yale, a licence in philosophy from the University of Paris I, and a Ph.D. from the London School of Economics, where his thesis was on the politics of innovation in communications technology.

events.title: Fascism After Work: Post-Fordism, Abandonment, and Care
events.description: This work-in-progress seminar asks what fascism looks like after the eclipse of the factory as capitalism's organizing stage of exploitation. Delivered in the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections and near the first anniversary of Paolo Virno's death, the seminar returns to Virno's account of post-Fordism to track how immaterial labor—the shared linguistic, cognitive, and affective capacity Virno saw as a site of potential liberation—has become the privileged site of extraction and, for many, of organized abandonment. Bringing Virno into dialogue with Black studies (Ruth Wilson Gilmore especially), the seminar argues that today's political ambivalence—the same capacities that promise exodus also expose populations to premature death—demands a new diagnosis of fascism, one grounded not in discipline but in freedom, deregulation, and a disfigured abolitionism. As the midterms reopen the question of what kind of political order the United States is choosing, the seminar closes by asking what infrastructures of care and sociality might sustain good lives amidst labor's ruins.Lorenzo Fabbri is a McKnight Land-Grant Associate Professor of French and Italian at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities. Author of Cinema is the Strongest Weapon. Race-Making and Resistance in Fascist Italy (University of Minnesota Press, 2023).

events.title: Lia, Mira, Maria: Performance/Reading with Marília Garcia (2026 Brazilian Writer-in-Residence)
events.location: Spanish & Portuguese Library, 5125 Dwinelle, Level E
events.description: What are the stages of mourning? Which path should one follow: that of memory? That of the archive (papers, traces)? After the loss of her mother, Lia, and of a friend, Maria, the author is eventually led to the monotypes of the Swiss-born artist Mira Schendel, who lived in Brazil. In the 1960s, Mira would sit in her kitchen and "engrave," in the presence of friends, drawings on the backs of Japanese paper, making lines and writing letters on the reverse side of the paper with a pointed object. Through this and other material and manual processes (handling papers, sorting through photographs, taking up swimming), the book Lia, Mira, Maria seeks to move through the stages of mourning. It includes images from archives, artworks, and family photographs, composing a kind of personal album of mourning. The performance combines the reading of a text with the live projection of images. The performance will be in English and will be followed by a conversation between Marília Garcia and Nathaniel Wolfson. Marília Garcia is a poet, translator, and researcher at the Rui Barbosa Foundation. She is the author of, among other books, Câmera lenta (Companhia das Letras, 2017; Oceanos Prize), Expedição: nebulosa (Companhia das Letras, 2023), and Pensar com as mãos (WMF Martins Fontes, 2025). In English, her chapbook The territory is not the map, translated by Hilary Kaplan, was published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2017.

events.title: Seeing Through a Mirror: The 1948 War in the Eyes of the World
events.location: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art and Life, 2121 Allston Way, Berkeley, CA
events.description: Annual Diller Lecture Reception and Light Refreshments: 5:00-5:30pm Presentation and Conversation 5:30-7:00pm The 1948 Arab-Israeli War attracted attention from the highest levels of international society, state governments, transnational NGOs, journalism, and public opinion. Palestine and the emerging state of Israel functioned as both a mirror and a magnifier. Israel's establishment and the Palestinian Nakba were interpreted through countries' specific interests, histories, and cultures. These events also elicited tremendous passion. Palestine's mirroring and magnifying effects did not originate in 1948, but the events of that year drastically augmented them, and the patterns of global reaction remain with us to this day. To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/e1v2ubg7fkEif56n8)Derek Penslar is the William Lee Frost Professor of Jewish History and the Director of the Center for Jewish Studies (https://cjs.fas.harvard.edu/) at Harvard University. Derek previously taught at Indiana University, the University of Toronto, and the University of Oxford, where he was the inaugural holder of the Stanley Lewis Chair in Modern Israel Studies. Derek has published a dozen books, including Theodor Herzl: The Charismatic Leader (2020) and Zionism: An EmotionalState (2023). He is currently writing a book titled The War for Palestine, 1947-1949: A Global History. Derek is a past president of the American Academy for Jewish Research, a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, and an Honorary Fellow of St. Anne's College, Oxford. – If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in these events, please contact Jennifer Lipscomb at jlipscomb@berkeley.edu (mailto:jlipscomb@berkeley.edu?subject=Accommodation%20Needed%20for%20CJS%20Event) with as much advance notice as possible. events.title: Ver la memoria: una conversación con Queralt Solé y Espe Pons || Seeing Memory: A Conversation with Queralt Solé and Espe Pons
events.description: This event is part of ALBA (https://alba-valb.org/)'s events series, "Making Memory Visible: Anti-Fascism, UC Berkeley, and The Spanish Civil War (https://alba-valb.org/making-memory-visible-anti-fascism-uc-berkeley-and-the-spanish-civil-war/)" History and photography are practices concerned with time. Both transform the fleeting into a foothold for memory, thought, and action. Queralt Solé (https://dlcl.stanford.edu/people/queralt-sole-barjau) (historian at the University of Barcelona) and Espe Pons (https://espepons.com/) (photographer) discuss their work on the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) and its ongoing echoes. Underlying their conversation is the question of the gaze: who sees what, and what it means to have seen it. Landscapes, mass graves, monuments, archives, documents, people, and objects become materials through which to consider how the visible and the invisible are articulated, and how we might move beyond the immediate. Anchored in their most recent work on mass graves (Solé) and international women volunteers in the Spanish Civil War (Pons), the conversation explores the intersections between art and the social sciences and their shared efforts to make memory visible. Moderated by Dr. Luis Madrigal (Department of Film & Media) *This event is in Spanish*
