events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Vivian Feig, Stanford University | Engineering Piezoelectric Biomaterials Across Length Scales for Transient Bioelectronics
events.description: Abstract: Bioelectronic technologies hold immense potential for monitoring, stimulating, and interfacing with living systems, but realizing their full impact requires materials that are less invasive, more adaptive, and accessible for widespread use. Achieving this vision demands new approaches that address the entire device lifecycle: from sustainable sourcing of raw materials; to integration with soft and dynamic tissues; to maintaining stable function over operational lifetimes; and ultimately to safe degradation or removal. Biomolecules are attractive building blocks for this task. Certain amino acids and peptides can assemble into crystalline structures that combine piezoelectricity with abundant, biodegradable, and chemically tunable components. But several challenges must be addressed before these molecules can be used to build practically useful materials. In this talk, I will discuss how my group engineers biomolecule-based piezoelectric materials across length scales to tune key performance attributes like stability and sensitivity to specific deformation modes. This work lays the foundation for new transient bioelectronic sensors and energy harvesters built from simple, naturally occurring molecules. Bio: Dr. Vivian Feig (pronounced "F-eye-g") is the Reid and Polly Anderson Faculty Fellow, Gabilan Fellow, and Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering and, by courtesy, Materials Science and Engineering at Stanford University. She has a multi-disciplinary background with academic and industrial training in chemical, materials, mechanical, and biomedical engineering. She obtained her B.S. in Chemical Engineering from Columbia University in 2012 and then spent 3 years working in the petrochemicals industry in both scale-up and manufacturing. In 2020, she obtained her PhD. in Materials Science and Engineering from Stanford University as a National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate (NDSEG) fellow under the guidance of Prof. Zhenan Bao. Subsequently, she received the Schmidt Science Fellows postdoctoral fellowship, which allowed her to pivot into translational medical research and mechanical engineering by joining the labs of Prof. Giovanni Traverso and Prof. Robert Langer at MIT and the Brigham and Women's Hospital.

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Efficient Power Modeling of Processors Across Design Abstractions
events.description: As technology scaling slows, power has become the primary constraint on processor design. From embedded devices with tight energy budgets to datacenters facing thermal and operational limits, power efficiency now drives all architectural and design decisions. Designers need accurate power estimates early in the design process, but that accuracy is only guaranteed by gate-level analysis that are is slow for long and realistic workloads. In this talk I present my work on reducing the time required to produce a power estimate at each level of design abstraction. First I describe a gate-level power methodology and study how power estimates change as a design moves from RTL to final layout. Next I present ProxyLM, which uses large language models to select on-chip power proxy signals directly from RTL without simulation traces. I then discuss ProfilePoint, which samples fast architectural simulation to find the few intervals that need detailed power analysis. Finally, I combine these methods and compare them against the gate-level baseline to show which approach best fits each design question.

events.title: Composition Colloquium: Julius Dobos
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: TITLE:Spatial Composition: The New Frontier Composers have been using rhythm and melody for thousands of years; harmony for centuries. Musique concrète expanded the use of timbre some 75 years ago. Are we on the verge of another musical disruption? What if, using spatial location and movement as compositional tools, songwriters, composers, and producers not only mixed but composed in and for immersive systems? Can SPACE be considered a new element of music? Do spatial decisions made during the composition phase have an effect on the musical content itself? Do listeners respond differently to spatially composed music than to immersive mixes of non-spatial concepts? How should one approach writing in an immersive environment to yield conceptually novel musical content? Based on his latest research in spatial composition and reflecting the global interest among music professionals in its findings, this presentation and immersive demonstration by composer Julius Dobos explores the use of spatial location and movement in music composition and production.

events.title: "The Smallest Unit of Liberation": Kuleana, Community, & Movement Building with Dr. Jamaica Heolimeleikalani Osorio
events.description: Register here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSck0HiXajzxnYA-1toomi9Q11AQkUjSVXio5GojYDxBJDbh-g/viewform?usp=dialog). Please note that space is limited. Confirmation information will be shared upon registration and as capacity allows."The Smallest Unit of Liberation": Kuleana, Community, and Movement Building This two-part workshop explores how we build movements rooted in deep relationships, collective responsibility, and intentional strategy. Grounded in the premise articulated by @eroticsofliberation that "relationships are the smallest unit of liberation," we begin by strengthening our understanding of kuleana—our responsibilities to one another, our communities, and the lands that sustain us. We then turn to the practical work of developing campaigns, sharpening our organizing strategies, and building the collective power necessary to win. Because liberation is not something we achieve alone, we must learn not only how to fight together, but how to build the relationships and movements that can sustain that fight.Part One: How Does Your Kuleana Move You? In this hands-on writing workshop, we will use poetry and storytelling to explore the many layers of kuleana, including our responsibilities to ourselves, our families, our lands, and our communities, as well as the privileges and obligations that shape how we show up in movement work. Through guided writing exercises, we will map our relationships, reflect on how we care for what we hold dear, and practice bringing those commitments to life through storytelling. No prior writing experience is necessary—just a willingness to reflect, imagine, and create. Participants will leave with a deeper understanding of the kuleana that shapes who we are, how we relate to one another, and how we move in the world.Part Two: Kiaʻi Basics—Campaigns, Strategy, and the Work of Getting Free Made possible through the movement training and organizing experience of SOUL, RUKUS Society, and the Huli Movement, this truncated facilitated learning workshop gets into the nitty-gritty of building effective campaigns and movements. We will explore the relationships between strategy, tactics, targets, messaging, and security culture, asking how these elements work together to build power and advance our collective struggles. Through discussion and practical exercises, we will examine not only what it takes to organize a campaign, but how to make strategic decisions, respond to challenges, and build movements capable of sustaining themselves over time.Dr. Jamaica Heolimeleikalani Osorio is a Kanaka Maoli organizer, artist, scholar, and public intellectual whose work is rooted in aloha ʻāina and the struggle for collective liberation. Born and raised in Hawaiʻi, Jamaica is a longtime participant in movements for Kanaka ʻŌiwi sovereignty, land and water protection, demilitarization, decolonization, and is the Vice President the Hawaiian National organization of Hui Aloha ʻĀina o Honolulu. Her organizing, teaching, and creative work are grounded in a belief that movements are sites of knowledge-making and that another world is not only possible, but already being built through collective action. Jamaica is also an Associate Professor of Indigenous and Native Hawaiian Politics at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where she teaches and writes at the intersections of Indigenous sovereignty, abolition, militarism, and collective liberation. Her work moves across the boundaries of scholarship, poetry, film, and movement organizing. She is the author of the award-winning Remembering Our Intimacies: Moʻolelo, Aloha ʻĀina, and Ea (https://www.nativebookshawaii.org/products/remembering-our-intimacies) (University of Minnesota Press, 2021) and her poetry and activism are the subject of the award-winning film This Is the Way We Rise (Sundance 2021). She was also a lead artist and co-writer of the award winning VR documentary On the Morning You Wake (To the End of the World) (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KyTb_56XzN8) (Premier:Sundance 2022 and XR Experience Jury Award at SXSW). Across these forms, Jamaica's work asks what it means to build liberatory futures from the places, relationships, and movements that have survived colonial violence. She writes and organizes toward a world grounded in aloha ʻāina, collective responsibility, Indigenous sovereignty, abolition, and abundance—and toward movements powerful enough to make that world real.

events.title: Fizzah Sajjad | Speculation and Circulation: Real Estate Development and the Market for Land in Urban Pakistan
events.description: The S. S. Pirzada Lecture on Pakistan by Fizzah Sajjad (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6784), the winner of the S. S. Pirzada Dissertation Prize for 2025 for her dissertation titled, Speculation and Circulation: Real Estate Development and the Market for Land in Urban Pakistan (London School of Economics and Political Science, 2025).Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Fri, Nov 6, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABSTRACT: This dissertation studies the dynamics of Lahore's rapidly expanding residential real estate market as a means to contextualize and understand growing housing pressures in the city. Specifically, it examines developer motivations and mechanisms of profitmaking to uncover why and how expansion has taken place in recent years, and in whose interests. By studying and centring the actions of supply side actors such as real estate developers, whose activities and modes of profitmaking remain understudied and undertheorized within existing scholarship, it investigates why the city's real estate market remains inaccessible for a majority of the city's residents. Drawing on sixteen months of fieldwork, this dissertation shows that actors in the business of land development in Lahore have devised a mechanism that overcomes constraints in accessing institutional finance and allows them to profit off land conversions without using their own resources. This mechanism – what I characterize as accumulation by speculative circulation – relies on market-making techniques and the circulation of a market-based instrument of land acquisition and sales known as 'the file' to finance land conversions. The file, as I show, is an object but also a future. It is a fictional commodity that turns 'land' into 'liquid' form, helping create a real estate market that is structured, first and foremost, to accommodate the interests of investors and state actors, rather than those looking to meet their housing needs. This thesis argues that the valorisation and repurposing of land for investment purposes serves as both site and mechanism of housing exclusion, contributing to spatial inequality in the city and heightening the odds against more equitable interventions. It also shows how state entities themselves are implicated in this accumulation model, and remain invested in furthering sprawl, gentrification and dispossession. By illustrating how speculative practices operate in real estate markets, especially in contexts where theory expects otherwise, the thesis contributes empirically and theoretically to questions of land commodification and peri-urban transformations, particularly in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. It also extends and complicates theories of speculative urbanisms, financialization and dispossession. SPEAKER BIOFizzah Sajjad i (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6784)s an Assistant Professor at the Lahore University of Management Sciences. Her research focuses on questions of land, housing, transport and the politics of infrastructure development in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. Fizzah holds a PhD in Human Geography and Urban Studies from the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) where her dissertation looked at speculative practices in residential real estate and the market for land in Lahore, Pakistan. She also has a Masters in City Planning from MIT.Her work has been published in leading journals including Antipode and Environment & Planning D, and she has co-edited the volume "Lahore in Motion: Infrastructure, History and Belonging in Urban Pakistan" (UCL Press, 2025). Fizzah also contributes to public scholarship through media outlets such as Dawn, Himal South Asia, and Jamhoor. Most recently, she was Co-Investigator on the project 'Navigating the grid in the 'world-class city: poverty, gender and access to services in India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka,' under the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) GCRF '(Re)Thinking the Off-Grid City' programme. This work examined how the urban poor access basic services in South Asian cities. The Pakistan sub-project more specifically explored peri-urban expansion in the city of Lahore, focusing on transformations and service provision challenges in formerly rural 'urban villages' that are now surrounded and encircled by suburban residential real estate projects. events.title: Film Screening: Harakiri
events.description: Masaki Kobayashi harnesses the breathtaking beauty of black-and-white, widescreen cinematography to create an abstract epic. Starring Tatsuya Nakadai, the film depicts one man's desperate attempt to crack the blind, absolute authority that characterizes the feudal age and, Kobayashi suggests, our own. In an Edo-period mansion, the camera inches down hallways and finds rooms within rooms to explicate a complex flashback narration. In the bloody climax, the black-robed figures who were caught and dissected by a stationary camera throughout the film come into their own as an inexorable prophecy, like Toru Takemitsu's haunting music and the words that emerge almost rhythmically from the dialogue: harakiri . . . (seppuku).

events.title: Film Screening: Kwaidan
events.description: Breathtakingly photographed on hand-painted sets, Kwaidan is at once a Japanese woodcut writ large, and an abstract wash of luminescent colors that seem to come from another world. An electronic soundtrack by avant-garde composer Toru Takemitsu plays hauntingly with natural sounds—crickets, rain, the cracking of wood, the loud silence of snow. Yet the stories—four of Lafcadio Hearn's ghostly tales—strangely contradict this plastic splendor in their simple, aching humanity. All are tales of mortals caught by forces beyond their comprehension when the supernatural world intervenes in their lives. This version of Kwaidan is the original three-hour Director's Cut.

events.title: Film Screening: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love
events.description: It is rare when an episode of national history can be interpreted without the burden of illusions, both obsolete and nostalgic. This is one of the great strengths of Masaki Kobayashi's The Human Condition, a nine-hour epic about Japan's occupation of China during World War II. The trilogy begins with an attack on inhuman practices in the Japanese army and ends with a bitter denunciation of Stalinism by the would-be-socialist hero, Kaji (the great Tatsuya Nakadai), a Japanese soldier who has confronted the reality of war and found it unyielding. In grand Dostoyevskian flourishes, Kobayashi suggests the impossibility of an individual altering the ethical standards of a social system. Standing in for the director, Kaji says, "Minor facts ignored by history can be fatal to the individual." It is Kobayashi's recognition of "minor facts" that joins the poetic to the journalistic in a scathing epic about the cruelties of war. This first part of the trilogy finds Kaji working as a supervisor in a forced labor camp in southern Manchuria, where he and his wife attempt to better the lot of the enslaved Chinese workers. Kaji is accused of dissent, tortured, and then inducted into the army.

Kobayashi’s monumental film can clarify and enrich your understanding of what it is to be alive” (New York Times).

events.title: Film Screening: Contempt
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director.

events.description: Speaker: Luis Daniel Abreu, University of ViennaWe construct a function Φ such that the orbit under the representation of $\Gamma = PSL(2,Z)$ is an orthonormal basis for the Bergman space with weight $q=12$. Moreover, we show that Φ is effectively computable as a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane (in the precise sense of computable analysis), by providing an effective procedure. This constructs a wandering and tracelike vector for $PSL(2,Z)$, whose abstract existence was proved by Sir Vaughan Jones in his last paper, where the corresponding construction was left as a problem. The construction of the function, which can also be represented as an orthonormal wavelet in the half-line, reproduces the method used in the signal approximation practice: the off-diagonal decay of the Gramian operator allows to control its restriction to nested finite subsets of $PSL(2,Z)$, where it becomes a finite matrix and can be inverted, leading to a convergent sum where all objects and bounds are computable in the cyclotomic field generated by the 12th-root of unity over the rationals. Since modular actions on the Bergman kernel enter the construction, Φ displays Bergman and modular reminescences, despite appearing to be modular itself. As suggested by Jones, it provides a computable implementing vector for th abstract anti-isomorphism between the von Neumann algebra $M_{12} (\Gamma )$and its commutant. With minor adaptations, the construction works for any cocompact Fuchsian group, but the more involved proof of computability is only executed for $PSL(2,Z)$.

events.title: IES Rapid Response | Student Protests in France
events.description: Hundreds of thousands of people have engaged in protest across France since mid September. The movement started with high school students dissatisfied with overcrowded, decrepit classrooms, missing teachers, and an opaque university placement system that seemed to work against the disadvantaged. Parents, teachers, labor unions, and members of local government have joined the high school students. The backdrop for these protests is a program of economic liberalization pursued by French president Emmanuel Macron since 2017 that combined tax cuts with reduced spending on public services including education. Join us for a rapid response lecture by expert in French politics and economic liberalization, Professor Jonah Levy, for a deep dive into the issues animating the student protests in France and the implications of these protests for the French economy and society as well as for far-right and far-left parties in the upcoming 2027 elections. Professor Jonah D. Levy teaches courses in the areas of comparative political economy, welfare policy, French and West European politics, and the politics of dystopian novels. In 2023, Levy published Contested Liberalization: Historical Legacies and Contemporary Conflict in France (Cambridge University Press, 2023), which describes and analyzes the contentious politics surrounding economic liberalization in France. In 2025, Levy published Rethinking Economic Liberalization (Edward Elgar), which traces progressive opportunities within liberalizing reforms. Levy has received a Phi Beta Kappa award for excellence in teaching and been selected as the UC Berkeley, Undergraduate Political Science Association Professor of the Year.Photo Credit: The Wallstreet Journal, https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/france-offers-concessions-to-quell-student-protests-2e164758 (https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/france-offers-concessions-to-quell-student-protests-2e164758)If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description: Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Path-Dependent Ergodic Optimal Control and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (Nizar Touzi, NYU)
events.description: Title: Path-Dependent Ergodic Optimal Control and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations Abstract: We investigate a new class of infinite-horizon backward stochastic differential equations for ergodic optimal control where the cost and state dynamics are time and path-dependent. The state process is defined on an unbounded underlying domain and satisfies an extended dissipativity condition. In contrast with the time-homogeneous Markovian setting, the optimal ergodic cost in our framework is characterized by the asymptotic behavior of a deterministic function, rather than by a single real constant. We obtain well-posedness, verification and stability properties, which extend the previous results in the literature on the Markov case. Bio: Nizar Touzi is a Professor at New York University, Chair of the Department of Finance and Risk Engineering at the Tandon School of Engineering. He has been an invited session speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians (Hyderabad 2010). He received the Louis Bachelier Natixis prize of the French Academy of Sciences in 2012, the Paris Europlace prize of Best Young Researcher in Finance in 2007, and he was awarded an Advanced ERC grant 2012-2017. He is co-editor and associate editor in various international journals in the fields of financial mathematics, applied probability, and control theory.

events.title: Robert Saxton (Chemistry/MCB Seminar): "Decoding the Molecular Logic of Tissue-Intrinsic Inflammatory Signaling"
events.description: Inflammation is regulated not only by immune cells, but also by receptor signaling circuits within tissues themselves. Epithelial and stromal cells produce cytokines that act locally on neighboring cells or feed back on the producing cells to regulate tissue responses to injury and inflammation. However, the molecular mechanisms governing these tissue-intrinsic signaling pathways, and their role in chronic inflammatory disease, remain poorly understood. In this talk, I will discuss our work on two epithelial cytokines, IL-24 and IL-17C. Combining structural biology, protein engineering, and mouse models, we are investigating how these cytokines engage their receptors to regulate tissue inflammation, as well as how this knowledge can guide the development of new therapeutics for chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics (Joint with Theory): David Dillenberger "Pure Risk"
events.description: Abstract: We introduce a behavioral notion of domain-specific risk aversion that separates attitudes toward risk from deterministic utility: an agent is more pure risk averse in one domain than in another if, for prizes that are indifferent under certainty, he is more averse to risk in the former domain than in the latter. We develop a model that goes beyond expected utility by allowing risk attitudes to vary across domains, while preserving expected utility within each domain. The domains are subjective and need not be specified in advance; they are identified from choice behavior. We establish uniqueness of the model's parameters and provide an axiomatic characterization. Paper Link: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7342358 (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id%3D7342358&source=gmail-imap&ust=1791993757000000&usg=AOvVaw2PzujPEXNQFPUv9FYn_2Be)

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information
events.description: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information Abstract: Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms. Biography: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: Sunrise Lecture by Leif Weatherby: "Has Reason Finally Actually Lost Its Mind?"
events.description: As the Cold War ended, a prominent group of scholars told the story of how reason had "almost lost its mind" in the excesses of Game Theory and optimization. According to that story, the episode was bizarre and dangerous, but had more or less dissipated along with the Soviet Republics. The idea of a quantitative rationality, an automatic basis for executing social judgments, had splintered into various disciplines and quieted down. We know today that this is not what happened. Out-of-control Bayesians and other so-called "rationalists" are in control of technology, markets, and even policymaking, writing what amounts to science fiction about a reason far more literally automated - superceding the human mind - than any rational choice or decision theorist could have dreamed. The ideology of perfectly automated reasoning now also has "evidence" in the form of AI models that scour the written record for solutions to mathematical conjectures and clever ways to commit random cybercrimes. This talk argues that reason was never in possession of the type of mind implied by the earlier, triumphalist stories of the historians of science, and turns to the philosophy of culture that traces from German Idealism to the present to recast the problem of reason in the age of AI. Leif Weatherby is the director of the Digital Theory Lab and Professor of German at New York University. He writes about systems of representation, especially computation and language, especially in their cultural aspects. His book, Language Machines, about AI and literary theory, appeared in 2025. He is currently a fellow of the Ideas Workshop of the Open Society Foundations working on a new book titled The Mismeasure of Mind: Against the Prediction of Everything. There is a workshop that goes with this lecture on November 10th, 10 am. Sign up here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScrZwzVwX9zV5RIxmih3fINUcClvefUOyZdND9gvs3vjz07oQ/viewform).

events.title: The Bomb in/and/out of the Archive. feat. Zoé Samudzi
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture with Zoé Samudzi Postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at Ohio State University - Monday, November 9, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeykJAzTsXRPcjwOetCQvBjTYgUR_hNZbyFZzKTNKnwucsB-Q/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MHRhNmwwNmJwZGxrMGFvZjlkZ3M5MG1xc2IgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Begun during her 2026 residency at La Becque in Switzerland, Zoé Samudzi presents the inaugural project of the research constellation "Can the African Steal?" Through archival photographs of the Belgian Congo (c. 1929-30) at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, Samudzi stitches together a variegated visual forensic through image absence through the deployment of the black planetary (after Canham and Seedat) as an onto-epistemic and transnational geographic frame. The negative spaces in the Swiss archive enable a positively articulated materiality of the atomic bomb. Her tracing of uranium extraction and/as warcraft conjoins King Leopold's free state and the Katangese mines in the Belgian Congo, the Trinity test in Los Alamos and Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and nuclear afterlives in Japan. About Zoé Samudzi Zoé Samudzi is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at The Ohio State University. She holds a PhD in Medical Sociology from the University of California, San Francisco. Her research contends with genocide memory and the multiplicity of denialisms, political mythologies of the postcolonial African state, visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing and witnessing, and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. An art critic and writer, Samudzi is an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine, a popular magazine dedicated to psychoanalytic thinking. She is a 2026 Public Parking editorial resident, a 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom," a 2026 resident at La Becque's Principal Residency Program, and an awardee of the 2026 Fire Station Studios' International Curator Residency.

events.description: Join us for a screening of Frontline's new award-winning documentary One in a Million. Filmed over 10 years, it follows Israa's epic journey from Syria to Germany and back again. She and her family navigate war, exile, and heartbreak in a foreign land, revealing the complexities of the refugee experience. After the film, producer and Frontline Editor-In-Chief Raney Aronson-Rath will discuss the film and take questions. Snacks will be available before the screening in the lobby. RSVP HERE (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeWjaO2EXvnExACSuCMOGInO8-TQ4f1rSaYPWarYbBSZu61cg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). In September 2015, filmmakers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa, an 11-year-old Syrian girl selling cigarettes on a street corner in Turkey, alongside her father, Tarek. The family had fled Aleppo to join the largest movement of people since the Second World War. Together they trekked through Eastern Europe before finding refuge in Germany, where more than one million asylum seekers were registered by the end of that year. For ten years, the filmmakers continued to document Israa's life as the challenges of integration and cultural adjustment led to family breakdown as Western culture clashed with Syrian traditions. Following the fall of the Assad regime in 2025, the film culminates when the filmmakers follow Israa, now a mother herself, back to the ruins of Aleppo as she confronts her own questions of identity and belonging. The film is a Sundance Winner for both the 'Audience Award: World Cinema Documentary' and the 'World Cinema Documentary Directing Award'.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marc Hillmyer, McKnight Presidential Endowed Chair, University of Minnesota Telechelic polymers for sustainable polyolefins Polyolefins are ubiquitous. They are lightweight, strong, and stable. These features render them useful in countless applications. Unfortunately, these attributes also contribute to the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in the environment. While polyolefins can be mechanically recycled, often this results in an inferior product and is in part the reason that only a small percentage of polyolefin products are effectively recycled. We have embarked on an effort to prepare polyolefins with functional groups at their chain ends. These telechelic polyolefins can be stitched together to form high molar mass plastics and thermosets. By virtue of the synthetic pathway used to make these materials, we generate products that include weak links along the backbones of the polymer chains. These links can be chemically cleaved to quantitatively deconstruct the material and allow for efficient chemical recycling back to the starting telechelic polymers that can be subsequently repolymerized. Our approach takes advantage of a tandem catalysis strategy that is perfectly atom economic and readily scalable. In this lecture I will discuss the preparation of the telechelic polyolefins and their use in the preparation of degradable polyolefin-based plastics and thermosets. I will also report on their materials properties, scalability, and recyclability.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Rachel Rutishauser: Targeting virus-specific CD8+ T cells to cure HIV
events.description: Antigen-specific CD8+ T cells are a key component of antiviral defense. Due to chronic antigen exposure, HIV-specific CD8+ T cells in the majority of people living with HIV are dysfunctional (poor effector function and proliferative capacity). However, they are highly functional and may mediate viral control in the rare individuals who control the infection spontaneously and are therefore an attractive target for immunotherapies seeking to achieve durable HIV remission in the absence of antiretroviral therapy. We will discuss T cell-intrinsic regulatory programs that promote HIV-specific CD8+ T cell function and dysfunction and new approaches being tested in pre-clinical and clinical settings to enhance HIV-specific CD8+ T cell function.This seminar is partially sponsored by NIHDivision(s): Division of Immunology and Molecular Medicine

events.title: Recovery from Democratic Backsliding: Lessons From—and For—Europe, with Prof. Tom Ginsburg (Chicago)
events.organizer: Miller Institute for Global Challenges and the Law
events.description: Institute for European Studies Director’s Theme Lecture Series for 2026-2027: Democracy in Peril This year’s election in Hungary ending 16 years of Viktor Orban’s rule raises important questions about the tactics of recovery from backsliding in Europe and around the world. Questions of sequencing, institutional redesign, and the balance between looking backward and forward have come to the fore, echoing the democratic transitions of 35 years ago. Are the answers different? Drawing on the experience of several countries, this lecture argues that today’s transitions raise distinct challenges and require different tools those of the prior generation. Shoring up the core institutions and practices of constitutional democracy is the immediate challenge. Tom Ginsburg is the Leo Spitz Distinguished Service Professor of International Law at the University of Chicago, where he serves as Faculty Director for the Forum on Free Inquiry and Expression, as well as the Malyi Center for the Study of Institutional and Legal Integrity. He holds B.A., J.D. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of California at Berkeley, and currently co-directs the Comparative Constitutions Project, an NSF-funded data set cataloging the world’s constitutions since 1789, that runs the award-winning Constitute website. The second edition of his book with Aziz Huq, How to Save a Constitutional Democracy has just been published, and he is the author of numerous other volumes on comparative constitutional studies and international law. He currently serves a senior advisor on Constitution Building to International IDEA and is also on the faculty of the American Bar Foundation. He also serves as the head of the MIT Data Science Lab. (https://dsl.mit.edu/) He is considered one of the premier thought leaders in supply chain management and business analytics. His Ph.D. students have accepted faculty positions in leading academic institutes including U. of California Berkeley, Carnegie Mellon U., Columbia U., Cornell U., Duke U., Georgia Tech, Harvard U., U. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, U. of Michigan, Purdue U. and Virginia Tech. In 2023, he was elected a member of the National Academy of Engineering. In 2020, he was awarded the prestigious INFORMS Impact Prize for playing a leading role in developing and disseminating a new highly impactful paradigm for the identification and mitigation of risks in global supply chains. He is an INFORMS Fellow and MSOM Distinguished Fellow and the recipient of the 2020 INFORMS Koopman Award given to an outstanding publication in military operations research; Ford Motor Company 2015 Engineering Excellence Award; 2014 INFORMS Daniel H. Wagner Prize for Excellence in Operations Research Practice; 2014 INFORMS Revenue Management and Pricing Section Practice Award; and 2009 INFORMS Revenue Management and Pricing Section Prize. He was the founder of LogicTools which provided software solutions and professional services for supply chain optimization. LogicTools became part of IBM in 2009. In 2012 he co-founded OPS Rules, an operations analytics consulting company. The company became part of Accenture in 2016. In 2014, he co-founded Opalytics, a cloud analytics platform company focusing on operations and supply chain decisions. The company became part of the Accenture Applied Intelligence in 2018.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: John Eiler, Robert P. Sharp Professor of Geology and Geochemistry, CaltechExploring the organic chemistry of the early solar system using molecular isotopic structureOrganic chemistry is ubiquitous across extraterrestrial environments and dominates the processing and delivery of carbon and nitrogen to rocky planetary bodies. Extraterrestrial settings and materials also present the most clearly revealed and diverse collection of constraints on the ways in which 'prebiotic' chemistry takes its first steps towards life. Some of the most detailed and nuanced constraints on this subject come from the laboratory study of the thousands of organic compounds sampled by carbonaceous meteorites and returned samples of asteroids. However, detailed understanding of these materials has been challenging because they may be intimate mixtures of the products of chemistry operating across many settings and processes. I will explore the origin and evolution of early solar system organic materials through application of molecular isotopic structure — the study of the distributions of naturally occurring rare isotopes (D, 13C, 15N, etc.) at scales of individual atomic positions and considering the very rare versions of molecules that contain two or more rare isotopes. These studies were enabled by more than two decades of inventions in mass spectrometry, studies of the chemical physics of previously unexamined isotopic forms of molecules, and applications to meteorites, returned samples, ancient earth materials and their laboratory analogues. The results reveal the long, complex journey of carbon and other volatile materials from synthesis in the interstellar medium, through the early history of the protoplanetary disk and into the 'prebiotic cauldron' of solar system bodies.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description: A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. events.title: Performance: Breath in this World
events.description: Join us at the Arts Research Center for Breath in this World, a solo performance of spoken word, sung voice, and body by poet, artist, and performer Aine Nakamura. About the work: The moon holds no light of its own. It receives the sun's light while the earth's shadow reshapes it. Two years ago, Nakamura began to consider the moon's shape as a membrane between stories, between inside and out. Since then, its swaying line and rings of light have led her toward questions of soul, wounds, and the human eye. In this work she follows light and darkness, line and shape through voice and breath. Premiered in March 2026 at Indexical in Santa Cruz, Breath in this World has traveled to the UCSD Music Spring Festival, ZK/U Berlin, Baiju Theatre near Beijing, UrBANBUILD in Kyoto, and Chicago. It continues to evolve through each performance and the time shared with audiences, who help shape what it means to see. About the artist:Aine Nakamura, is a performer of voice and body, poet, and artist. She focuses on the potentialities of an injured voice and the listening and sensing bodies. She often writes words and considers shapes as if her throat is a membrane and each body part is a shape, phenomenon among worldly phenomena, in relations. Through her practice, while aiming to be a vessel, she understands about herself and pursues meanings of lines, seeing and connecting. She is a PhD candidate at UC Berkeley and is based in the Bay Area/East Bay, presenting works locally and internationally. Her recent works include solo performance "Breath in this World" premiered at Indexical in SC, which continues to evolve at ZK/U Berlin, Baiju Theater near Beijing, UrBANGUILD in Kyoto, Chicago, and will be presented at Arts Research Center; month-long site-specific exhibition and performance project "hands on tape," presented at The Lab in SF; solo performance "Under an Unnamed Flower" during an invitation to the 50th International Theatre Festival at the Venice Biennale; solo multiple performance project "Circle hasu We plant seeds in the spring of mountains" presented at Theatertreffen at Berliner Festspiele after its premiere at the Gallatin Galleries in NY. She also engages in listening and walking in relation to long-term soul work, which resulted in her performance at The Listening Biennial Singapore. In exploring the presence of wounds and repair, she seeks the concepts of fragile kindness and love to access pathways to vulnerability. She is also a committed collaborator and improviser, through which she develops her approach to attunement, spaces and listening.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Fractional eigenvalue escape rates on quantum graphs, and a Hermitian preparation theorem
events.description: Speaker: Gregory Berkolaiko, Texas A&M UniversityTake a quantum graph with a core whose edges have length of order s, attach a few infinite leads, and let s go to 0. Some negative eigenvalues will run off to -infinity, and an a priori bound says they cannot go faster than \(s^{-1}\). Simple examples show that this bound is sharp. Surprisingly, an eigenvalue can also escape at the rate \(s^{-2/3}\). Nothing in the problem (the Laplacian, the vertex conditions, the edge lengths) contains a cube root. So which other strange rates are possible?The answer turns out to be: none. For any graph and any fixed self-adjoint vertex conditions there are exactly two escape rates, \(s^{-1}\) and \(s^{-2/3}\). The number of eigenvalues of each kind, and their leading coefficients, can be read off explicitly from the vertex conditions.The proof turns the problem into the study of the zero set of an analytic function of two variables, and that brings tools from algebraic geometry into play. The Newton–Puiseux theorem tells us that solution branches follow fractional powers; the difficult part is to show that only two powers are possible. The key tool is a Hermitian matrix version of the Weierstrass preparation theorem, recently proved by Nils Dencker. It leads to an "implicit Rellich theorem": the solutions of a certain class of Hermitian determinantal equations in two variables behave like the eigenvalues of a one-parameter Hermitian family; in particular, they are analytic, as in Rellich's classical theorem. I will explain this result, which may be useful elsewhere, and show how it produces the two rates.Joint work with Denis Borisov, Marshall King and Julien Royer.

events.title: A collections-based approach to bryophyte diversity and disjunct distributions between the Neotropics and Africa
events.description: How do we explain patterns of biodiversity when our knowledge of species and their distributions is incomplete? Despite their diversity and ecological importance, bryophytes remain poorly documented across much of the tropics, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of where species occur and why. Historical herbarium collections offer opportunities to reveal overlooked diversity, refine our knowledge of species distributions, and investigate the ecological and evolutionary processes shaping regional floras. Realizing this potential requires attention to both the specimens themselves and the histories of collecting and access that shape our knowledge.In this seminar, I will talk about three connected themes in my ongoing collections-based research on bryophytes in Madagascar, sub-Saharan Africa, and the Neotropics. The first focuses on how revisiting historical collections can reveal previously unreported species occurrences and inform our understanding of species richness and endemism. The second focuses on the "silent herbaria" of sub-Saharan Africa: how the history of botanical exploration, the visibility of local collections, and their representation in digital resources such as GBIF influence our understanding of bryophyte diversity. This raises a fundamental challenge for ecological inference: distinguishing biological patterns from gaps in collecting and access to knowledge. The third addresses bryophyte species with disjunct distributions between the Neotropics and Africa. Integrating herbarium specimens, genomic data, and spatial modelling provides a framework for testing hypotheses about long-distance dispersal, historical isolation, and intercontinental gene flow, and for examining how niche evolution shapes colonization and diversification across continents.

events.title: Under Pressure: Attitudes Towards China Among American Foreign Policy Professionals | Lecture by Rory Truex
events.description: How do social norms and professional incentives affect policy discourse within the Washington foreign policy community? We conducted over 50 semi-structured interviews and a survey of nearly five-hundred American foreign policy and national security professionals about their views towards the People's Republic of China. Over one fifth of survey respondents noted instances of professional pressure to voice a more hawkish point of view towards China, and many feared being perceived as naive or compromised by their views on, ties to, and experiences in China. These pressures were particularly acute for foreign policy professionals that are traditionally marginalized from power–those who are younger, non-white, or female. Our interview subjects reported a number of different coping strategies, including trying to communicate their views in the language of the perceived consensus. This "discourse mirroring" is distinct from preference falsification and self-censorship but may still contribute to difficulties in gauging peoples' true attitudes. Speaker BioRory Truex is Associate Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton, where his research and teaching focuses on authoritarianism. He is the host of Civic Forum, a podcast about the big questions facing democracy, in the US and elsewhere.

events.description: Sponsor(s):The Redwood Center (https://redwood.berkeley.edu/), Simons Institute (https://simons.berkeley.edu/homepage) Today's AI systems are powerful, but they work on principles very different from those of the human brain. They typically learn from large, static datasets, operate as black boxes, and need retraining for each new task. The brain, by contrast, learns continuously through active interaction with the world, builds structured models of what it senses, and generalizes across many kinds of tasks with remarkable efficiency. In this talk, Jeff Hawkins explains how the brain's sensorimotor principles allow it to understand the world, and why reverse-engineering the neocortex may provide a blueprint for a new kind of artificial intelligence. The Thousand Brains Project is an open-source effort to turn these principles into a practical framework for researchers and developers. Reception at 5:30pm, talk at 6pm. events.title: Laurent Warlouzet | Liberty, Solidarity and Community: Capitalism and European Integration, 1945 to the Present
events.description: How have European countries coped with the challenge of industrial capitalism and the rise of superpowers? Through an analysis of European integration from 1945 to the present day, Laurent Warlouzet argues that the European response was to create both new institutions, in particular the European Union, and an original framework of governance for capitalism. Beyond the European case, he demonstrates that capitalism is not just a contest between free marketeers and their opponents, those in favour of welfare and environmental policies, because there is a third camp that defends protectionism and assertive defence policies. Hence, the governance of capitalism has three foundational principles– liberty, solidarity, and community. The book explores debates among Europeans about how to address global interdependence in political, economic, and environmental terms. It is based on fresh archival evidence collected in eight countries. Laurent Warlouzet is professor of history at Paris Sorbonne Université. A former postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at the European University Institute (EUI), he works on the international economic history of the post-1919 period, particularly European integration and comparative European history. His previous monograph in English (Governing Europe in a Globalizing World, 2018) was reviewed in Foreign Affairs. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Capitalism. European integration and capitalism is an updated version of Europe contre Europe, originally published in French and reviewed in the mainstream media, including Le Monde, Le Grand Continent and Mediapart. The book will be published in German by Hamburger and in Italian by Luiss UP. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Community is available in open-access on the Cambridge UP here (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/liberty-solidarity-and-community/355531CFEE184AFF8B706B24D25EC368). events.title: Rahul Parson | Kathā-Kalkattā: Hindi Literature in a Bengali City
events.description: A talk by Rahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson), Assistant Professor of Hindi Literature and Culture, at UC Berkeley, that recovers Calcutta as a major center of Hindi literary production from the 1950s to the 1990s, showing how its multilingual archives complicate conventional linguistic geographies of Indian literature and illuminate questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition.Sukanya Banerjee (https://english.berkeley.edu/people/sukanya-banerjee), Associate Professor of English will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, November 16, 2026 (NOTE NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT Calcutta, Kolkata, Kalkattā: three names for one city, and the last one belongs to the Hindi and Urdu speakers who make up more than a third of its population. The conventional geography of Indian literature follows the linguistic boundaries drawn by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 — literary habitations of Bengali for Bengal, Hindi for north India, Tamil for Tamil Nadu — a map that effaces Hindi writing produced outside the Hindi belt. Calcutta has been a Hindi literary city for over two centuries, since Bengal gave Hindi its first printed newspaper. This talk takes up the decades from the 1950s to the 1990s, when writers, editors, and theatre-makers set out to define what a Calcutta Hindi literature might be. They compiled their own archives, collections, and critical practices: R̥shi Jaiminī Kauśika's Kalakattā ke Hindī kathākāra (1952), Sharad Deora's two-volume Mahānagar (1969), the annual Kalkattā (1985–98), the journal Aṇimā, named for the yogic power of becoming infinitesimally small, and Shyamanand Jalan's theatre group Anamika. What emerged was a literature shaped by contact and separation at once — from Bengali locally, and from the movements of the Hindi belt. Reading the city as a literary confluence rather than a single tradition changes our account of both Hindi literature and Calcutta. The map was drawn over the multilingual city; the paper trail shows what it covered. The archive poses questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition in Calcutta and similar global port cities. ABOUT THE SPEAKERRahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson) received an MA and PhD in the Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, with a specialization in Modern Hindi literature. Before returning to the Berkeley in 2021, he served as an Assistant Professor of Hindi and Urdu at the University of Colorado, Boulder (2016-2020) and a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter (Postdoctoral Researcher) at Max-Weber-Kolleg, Universität Erfurt, Germany (2014-2016). Rahul Parson's area of specialization is Hindi literature and literary history, with a particular emphasis on Hindi movements in Bengal. His book project, Confluences at the End of the Ganges: Modernity, Migration and Hindi Literature in Kolkata, fills in the Bengal portion of the map of Hindi studies. The monograph reveals the dynamism and syncretism of the hitherto overlooked world of Hindi literature in Bengal and the affective archives and narratives of migrants. It inaugurates research on the literatures of displaced and migrant peoples in South Asia by using cultural texts to explore the articulations of life-worlds of women and migrants. Additionally, he researches early-modern Jain poetry and philosophy, particularly the Jain adhyātma (spiritual or mystical) poetry. Dr. Parson participated as a core member of a research group based at the Max-Weber-Kolleg. In this capacity, he worked as a co-editor of a four-volume series entitled: Religious Individualisations: Historical Dimensions and Comparative Perspectives (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2020). events.title: The 2026 Emilio Segrè Lecture Featuring Francis Halzen: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South Pole
events.location: The Chevron Auditorium at International House
events.description: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South PoleFrancis Halzen, University of Wisconsin–Madison Abstract: The IceCube project at the South Pole melted 86 holes 2.5 kilometer deep in the Antarctic ice sheet to construct an enormous astronomical observatory that is also the largest neutrino detector ever built. The experiment discovered a flux of neutrinos from deep space with energies more than a million times those of neutrinos produced at accelerator laboratories like Fermilab. Some originate in the enigmatic cosmic particle accelerators that are the sources of cosmic rays. This lecture will discuss the IceCube neutrino telescope and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin. It will highlight the recent discovery that high-energy neutrinos—and cosmic rays—originate in sources powered by rotating supermassive black holes in active galaxies. With gravitational waves, high-energy gamma rays and neutrinos, IceCube launched multiparticle astronomy. Francis Halzen is a Vilas and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Born in Belgium, Halzen received his Master's and PhD degrees from the KU-Leuven, Belgium, and has been on the physics faculty at UW–Madison since 1972; in 2021, Halzen was named a Vilas Research Professor, one of the university's most prestigious honors. He has been a fellow of the American Physical Society since 1994 and a member of the US National Academy since 2024, and is the recipient of numerous awards, including the 2014 Smithsonian American Ingenuity Award, the 2015 Balzan Prize, a 2018 Bruno Pontecorvo Prize, the 2019 IUPAP Yodh Prize, the 2021 Bruno Rossi Prize, the 2021 Homi Bhabha Award, and honorary doctorates at several universities. Halzen is the Principal Investigator of IceCube, a cubic-kilometer neutrino telescope buried in the Antarctic ice at the South Pole. IceCube's first observations of high-energy cosmic neutrinos garnered the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award. In September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the direction of a blazar called TXS 0506+056. This was the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since they were discovered over one hundred years ago. Also a skilled science communicator, Halzen travels widely, giving about 20 or more invited talks per year at conferences, workshops, and colloquia. He also gives regular public talks to local and national groups and interviews for television and radio. Halzen is the co-author of Quarks and Leptons, a classic textbook on modern particle physics that continues to be used extensively throughout college campuses today. He has a large number of publications to his credit and has written or edited several other books. His essay "Antarctic Dreams," about the early days of AMANDA, IceCube's precursor, was featured in The Best American Science Writing 2000.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Founders and Their Heterogeneous Firms"
events.description: Abstract: Firm creation is at the heart of macroeconomic growth, but entrepreneurial outcomes are highly unequal. In this paper, we study the determinants of which entrants become large firms with macroeconomic importance. Using employer-employee-shareholder linked Canadian administrative data based on tax records, we find that workers with higher employment earnings are more likely both to enter entrepreneurship and to found larger firms with greater growth potential. We incorporate this link between founders' labor-market and entrepreneurial capacities into a quantitative model of endogenous occupational choice. In the presence of ex-ante heterogeneity, small business tax deductions induce negative selection by drawing lower-potential entrepreneurs into entry, largely oﬀsetting their positive eﬀects in alleviating financial frictions and generating a quantity-quality trade-oﬀ in the design of entrepreneurial policies.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: David Limmer, Professor, UC BerkeleyTitle: On the Stability and Function of Chemical Reaction NetworksThe remarkable complexity of living systems emerges from networks of chemical reactions that operate persistently far from equilibrium. These networks sustain stable states despite incessant fluctuations, reorganize in response to changing environments, and process information with extraordinary fidelity. Yet the physical principles that govern their stability and constrain their function remain poorly understood. Unlike equilibrium systems, where free energy provides a unifying organizing principle, nonequilibrium chemical networks lack a comparably general framework. Developing such a framework is a central challenge for modern statistical mechanics. In this talk, I will discuss advances in nonequilibrium theory connecting fluctuations, dissipation, stability, and function. First, I will describe a theory for the stability of reaction–diffusion systems based on the statistical mechanics of rare trajectories. Using instanton approximations and fluctuations around the most probable transition paths, we uncover how nonequilibrium driving and path entropy determine the relative stability of competing states. Second, I will consider biochemical signaling networks and introduce a general dissipation–error bound connecting the energetic cost of driving to the accuracy of responses to time-dependent signals. Together, these results reveal organizing principles that transcend specific molecular mechanisms, with broad implications for chemistry, materials science, and biology.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.description: A talk by Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a), Senior Lecturer in History at the Australian National University, drawing on a rare archive of family letters and remittances to examine the understudied history of Indian middle-class migration to Southeast Asia and the ways the Depression shaped mobility, economic insecurity, social isolation, and transimperial connections to home. Event moderated by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Nov 17, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–ABSTRACT: Studies of migration across the Bay of Bengal focus largely on the movement of millions of Tamil labourers between the second half of the 19th century and the 1930s to serve the demands of British imperial capital accumulation during the first era of globalization. While connected histories of South and Southeast Asia and memory point to "a large middling group of Indians, clerks in government and private offices, doctors, drivers, lower management in the oilwells and teak sawmills," shopkeepers, and traders (Bayly and Harper, 2005), they fail to say very much about this class of people because of their invisibility to the colonial archive. This paper begins to illuminate what has been hidden thus far. It draws chiefly on the author's collection of 500 pages of remittances and correspondences exchanged between his maternal grandfather P.K. "Java" Raman (1909-97) who migrated to work as a typist in Batavia (today's Jakarta) in the Dutch East Indies and his family members in the Malabar region of British India, between 1930 and 1934. The paper suggests the Depression as a period of migration rather than its eclipse; explores structures of feeling around economic insecurity and isolation of the thin stratum of Indian professionals in Southeast Asia; and sketches an earlier history of remittance between Indians overseas and in the homeland, across empires. Looking beyond the letters, it discusses possible sources and themes for microhistories of crossing the Bay of Bengal.ABOUT THE SPEAKER:Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a) is a Senior Lecturer at ANU's School of History, in the College of Arts and Social Sciences (CASS). Aditya's first book, Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2023), is a history of economic ideas and politics (UK/US link (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691205243/toward-a-free-economy) South Asia link (https://www.amazon.in/Toward-Free-Economy-Swatantra-Opposition/dp/0691256578)). It was shortlisted for the 2022 Elder Prize in the Social Sciences of the American Institute of Indian Studies and the 2024 W.K. Hancock Prize for best first monograph of the Australian Historical Association, and longlisted for the 2024 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Prize of the New India Foundation. A suite of peer-reviewed articles published over the last several years have interrogated various aspects of Indian political economy between the 1940s and the 1970s. Topics range from India's role in the international economic order, famine in Travancore during World War II, Hindu nationalist economic thought and policy, and anticorruption. He is currently working on two projects. The first is an environmental and economic history of roadbuilding and transport in India. Initial thoughts appeared in this post (https://histecon.fas.harvard.edu/climate-loss/roads/index.html) for the Harvard Center for History and Economics' "Visualizing Climate and Loss" blog in October 2023. During 2025-2028, he is the recipient of an Australian Research Council Discovery Early Career Research Award (DECRA) for this project. The second is a synthetic history of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984, the world's largest industrial disaster. This project is especially concerned with failures of relief and rehabilitation, chronic illnesses, and ongoing environmental pollution. He has just completed an article on forest management in India and is working on an article that sketches a revisionist history of migration between South and Southeast Asia. At ANU, Aditya teaches or has taught historical methods, environmental history, the history of political economy, and South Asian history. His teaching has been recognized with nominations for College and University-wide prizes. He is the Deputy Director of ANU's Center for Environmental History (https://history.cass.anu.edu.au/centres/ceh) and founded the ANU Capitalism Studies Network (http://csn.anu.edu.au/) with Will Bateman (Law) and Melinda Cooper (Sociology). He is completing a second term as Board Member of the South Asia Research Institute (2020-2021, 2024-6). From 2018 to 2024, he created and coordinated the Archives of Economic Life in South and Southeast Asia (https://www.histecon.magd.cam.ac.uk/archives-asia/index.html) website (you can learn more about it in this (https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/doing-online-south-southeast-asian-history/) Toynbee Prize Blog interview). events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Ignacio Navarrete
events.description: In Sneaking into Print (Toronto, 2026), Ignacio Navarrete (Spanish & Portuguese) explores the impact of early printing on narrative literature in Spain. He reveals how new technology enabled older texts and translations to circulate alongside newly written works, giving rise to a distinct narrative culture. Through an in-depth study of various narrative subgenres including hagiography, the epic, and sentimental fiction, Sneaking into Print integrates historical bibliography, material book features, and literary analysis. By examining texts as physical artifacts and narrative constructs, the book sheds light on their broader implications for narrative theory, offering fresh perspectives on the intersections of literature, materiality, and the early print marketplace. Navarrete is joined by Nicholas Paige (French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: International Court of Justice: Judicial Fellowship Panel
events.description: ICJ Judicial Fellowship Panel Wednesday, November 18 · 1:00 PM · Berkeley Law, Room 141 Each year, the International Court of Justice selects fifteen Judicial Fellows from hundreds of candidates nominated by law schools around the world to clerk at the Peace Palace in The Hague for ten months. Berkeley Law nominates up to four candidates each year and provides a significant fellowship stipend for any Berkeley nominee the Court selects. Join BJIL and ILS, with support from the Miller Institute, for a conversation with four recent Judicial Fellows: Félix Aguettant (Berkeley Law LL.M. ’23), Allyson Ping, Lara Manbeck, and Marina Wilbraham. They will talk about the application process, their time at the Court, and where the fellowship has taken them since. PANELISTS Félix Aguettant is a lawyer in the Legal Service of the European Commission, in the EU External Relations and International Law team, based in Brussels. He is also a PhD candidate in public international law at the Sorbonne. He was a 2024-25 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Abraham and H.E. President Iwasawa. He is an alumnus of Berkeley Law’s executive LLM program and was nominated to the fellowship by Berkeley Law in 2024. He is currently the head coach of Berkeley Law’s 2026-27 Jessup team. Félix is bilingual in English and French and is a member of the California Bar. To date, Felix is the only Berkeley Law alum to have ever been a judicial fellow! Allyson Ping is a litigation associate at Debevoise & Plimpton, New York. From 2024-2025, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. President Iwasawa Yuji. Allyson received a J.D. from Columbia Law School in 2024, where she was a member of the Jessup Moot Court team and was co-Executive Editor of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law. Lara Manbeck is an Associate at Covington & Burling in Washington, D.C. From 2025 to 2026, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. Judge Nolte and later as an Associate Legal Officer at the Court. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law, an MPhil from the University of Cambridge, and a B.A. from New York University. Prior to law school, she worked in the Office of the Director-General of the International Development Law Organization. Marina Wilbraham is currently a Law Clerk at White and Case LLP, in the firm’s LA office, where her practice focuses on international technology disputes. She was a 2025-2026 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Sarah H. Cleveland. Previously, she was an Associate at Debevoise & Plimpton LLP for two years in New York, in the Litigation Department, where she worked on a mix of international arbitration, public international law, and commercial litigation matters. Marina is a 2023 Yale Law School graduate. BERKELEY LAW’S JUDICIAL FELLOWSHIP APPLICATIONS Applications for the 2027–28 judicial fellowship, run by the CDO, will open in December 2026 and close in January 2027. Details about the 2026-27 application for Berkeley Law’s nomination process here. You can find details about the fellowship on the ICJ Judicial Fellowship website. JD and LL.M. students in the classes of 2025, 2026 and 2027 are eligible to apply, provided they meet other eligibility criteria of the Court. LUNCH Lunch will be provided if you RSVP here.
