events.title: Dylan Spaulding: The US Nuclear Paradigm Shift: Pit Production, Nuclear Testing, and the fate of Stockpile Stewardship
events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook The US nuclear weapons complex is undergoing its biggest transformation since the end of the Cold War. Increasingly sophisticated experimental, computational, and manufacturing techniques that emerged to support a strategy of science-based stockpile stewardship are now being applied as tools for vertical proliferation as emphasis shifts from ‘stewardship’ to production. The evolution of laboratory tools for weapons development comes with both challenges and opportunities for verification, nonproliferation, and disarmament. This talk will address the paradigm shift underway in the US and its implications for new plutonium pit production and the potential resumption of nuclear testing.

events.title: Bancroft Library Roundtable
events.description: The Bancroft Library holds the world's largest collection of George Sterling manuscripts, photographs, books, and biographical and critical materials. During the first quarter of the 20th century, Sterling was one of the most acclaimed poets in the U.S. Across his career, he wrote songs, plays, movies, short stories, essays, and more than a thousand poems. His works were published in many American literary magazines, in more than a hundred newspapers, in anthologies, and in his own books. To mark the 100th anniversary of his death, foremost Sterling experts S.T. Joshi, Ariadna García Carreño, and Vince Emery will reveal rarities that tell the surprising story of the poet and playwright.

events.title: Katherine Nagel: Understanding the logic of the fly navigation system
events.description: All animals need to navigate to find food and resources in their environment. My lab has been using odor-guided navigation to uncover the organization and logic of the fly navigation system. I will present recent and ongoing work aiming to describe how the fan-shaped body, a part of the fly navigation system thought to specify allocentric goal directions, organizes multi-sensory input and computes goals based on ongoing experience. One of our guiding interests is understanding what is similar and different across the navigation systems of different species. I hope this question inspires some interesting discussions!

events.title: Esha Niyogi De | Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia
events.description: A talk by Esha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/), Senior Lecturer in UCLA's Writing Programs, on her new book, Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p088285) (University of Illinois Press, December 2024). The book uncovers the overlooked histories of women who worked as producers, directors, performers, and "star-authors" across the film industries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. De examines how these women used stardom, collaboration, and creative labor to cross geographic, institutional, and gendered boundaries, claim greater authority over filmmaking, and challenge the structures that often obscured their contributions to South Asian cinema.Maya Sidhu (https://french.berkeley.edu/people/maya-sidhu), Lecturer in the Department of French and a scholar of film and media studies, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Thu, November 19, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOK This book talk delves into previously submerged histories and hidden voices of women directors and film entrepreneurs from Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Drawing on neglected archives and rare field interviews with filmmakers and fans, Esha tells a comparative story of women's creative authority and entrepreneurial labor in selected film industries of South Asia—industries and markets that share languages, arts, and geopolitical rifts. Using "transborder" to refer not only to territorial borders but also to institutional and conceptual ones, her story dwells on two eras of women's cinema in this postcolonial region. In the era of the "star-authors" (50s-90s), female stars in Dhaka, Lahore, and Kolkata perform personas ambiguously to access infrastructures and direct fiction films that breach sexual and national borders. In the era of the "woman director" (2000s), even though opportunities appear to burgeon across the region, women negotiate transnational borders that take less obvious forms of brand-making and censorship. The talk will include rare footage from fiction films made by Kohinoor Akhtar Suchanda, Babita, Nargis Akhter (Bangladesh), Shamim Ara (Pakistan), and Kanan Devi (India). SPEAKER BIOEsha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/)'s research interests lie in South Asian gender politics, film and performance history, and literary history. She is the author of two monographs, a recent study of women's cinemas in selected film industries of Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India titled Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (University of Illinois Press, 2024), and an earlier book on sexual politics and postcoloniality in literature, cinema, and choreography in the Bengal region titled Empire, Media, and the Autonomous Woman: A Feminist Critique of Postcolonial Thought (Oxford University Press, 2011). Other publications include two co-edited books, from University of Washington Press and Duke University Press, and many articles. She is working on two new book projects. The first, a study of the renowned Pakistani actress-singer and film director Noor Jehan in relation to Muslim nationalist arts in the mid-twentieth century, is titled Recasting Noor Jehan:Melody Queen, Film Pioneer, and the Making of National Cultures in South Asia (co-authored with Gwendolyn Sarah Kirk). The second, a comparative study of gendered choreographies of protest in twentieth century avant-garde and industrial films, made by Zahir Raihan, Satyajit Ray, Rangeela, among others, is tentatively titled Moving Bodies Out of Line: Filmic Choreographies, Protest Movements, and Queerness in South Asian Cinemas. Esha is a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Writing Programs at UCLA and a Faculty Affiliate of the UCLA Center for India and South Asia.EVENT POSTER _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. events.title: Earl L. Muetterties Lectures in Chemistry
events.description: Joesp Cornella, Director, Max-Plank InstituteExploring the Far Reaches of the Periodic Table: Bismuth Redox CatalysisThe success of transition metal catalysis in organic synthesis is rooted in decades of advances in fundamental organometallic reactivity. Bonding theory on d-block elements has allowed synthetic chemists to design novel and powerful catalysts that underpin modern chemical manufacturing. However, the increasing demand, cost, and environmental impact associated with many transition metals highlighted the need for alternatives. To this end, exploration of underutilized regions of the periodic table might reveal unconventional mechanisms inaccessible within established frameworks, making the search for sustainable alternatives a powerful driver of discovery. Beyond the transition metal realm lies a group of elements that have largely been overlooked by the synthetic community: the heavy elements, ignored by many due to the historically bad reputation associated to them. Yet, among them, one can find bismuth (Bi), placed at the fringe of the periodic table, virtually representing the last stable element. Bismuth is the main character of this talk, which will highlight how our laboratory unlocked its potential as redox catalyst for organic synthesis. Importantly, we will discuss how relativistic effects encoded in bismuth's electronic structure are the main driver in certain contexts, thus shaping the kinetic and thermodynamic landscapes of chemical reactions.Lecture 2 of 2

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis"
events.description: Please join us on Tuesday, November 24th from 4:00–5:30pm for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis by Matthew Shutzer, Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. Professor Shutzer will be joined in conversation by Youjin Chung, Associate Professor in the Department of Environmental Science, Policy & Management and the Energy & Resources Group at UC Berkeley, and Daniel Aldana Cohen, Assistant Professor of Sociology at UC Berkeley. The talk will be moderated by Michael Watts, Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Departments of South & Southeast Asia Studies and Geography, and the Energy and Resources Group.About the Book India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. In the book, Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.PanelistsMatthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching are concerned with the place of the environment in global history, with a particular focus on fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. He has also worked on topics that connect global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. He is currently at work on a second book project on climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945.Youjin B. Chung (https://youjinbchung.net/about) studies the relationship between gender and inequality, rural development, and socio-environmental change in East Africa, with a focus on Tanzania. The overarching question that drives her research program is: how and why do development policies and processes that aim to improve sustainability and equity outcomes often reinforce existing power structures and marginalize the groups they intend to serve? Over the years, she has channeled this central animating concern into three specific research projects. Using Tanzania as an analytic case, these projects investigate some of the most contentious issues in global development and environmental politics: large-scale farmland investments, sustainable livestock intensification, and the critical minerals rush. She is the author of Sweet Deal, Bitter Landscape: Gender Politics and Liminality in Tanzania's New Enclosures (Cornell University Press, 2024). At Berkeley, she convenes the Critical Ruralities Lab, a research workshop and collaborative mentoring space that promotes empirically grounded and justice-oriented scholarship on development and socio-environmental change in the global countryside.Daniel Aldana Cohen (https://aldanacohen.com/) is Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley, where he is Director of the Socio-Spatial Climate Collaborative, or (SC)2 (https://sc2.berkeley.edu/), and serves as a faculty affiliate in the graduate program on Political Economy. He is also Founding Co-Director of the Climate and Community Institute, a progressive climate and economy think tank. He has been a CIFAR Azrieli Global Scholar (2021-24) and Member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey (2018-19). He is the co-author of A Planet to Win: Why We Need a Green New Deal (Verso 2019). Cohen works on the intersections of the climate emergency, housing, political economy, social movements, and inequalities of race and class in the United States and Brazil. As Director of (SC)2, he is leading qualitative and quantitative research projects on Whole Community Climate Mapping, green political economy, and eco-apartheid. He was also co-founder and co-PI of the Superstorm Research Lab (https://superstormresearchlab.org/), in New York City.Michael Watts (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-emeritus-michael-watts) is Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. He served as the Director of the Institute of International Studies at Berkeley from 1994 to 2004 and was Director of Social Science Matrix at Berkeley in 2019–20. He was most recently a Non-resident Long-term Fellow at the Swedish Collegium for Advanced Study (SCAS). Watts is a member of the British Academy, was a Guggenheim Fellow in 2003, and was awarded the Victoria Medal by the Royal Geographical Society in 2004, and the Berlin Prize by the American Academy in Berlin in 2016. He was awarded the Ester Boserup Prize in 2024. Watts' writing has addressed a number of development issues especially famine and food security, political violence and the agrarian question in Africa, South Asia and Vietnam, natural resources and especially the energy and mineral sectors, and the political economy of development and governance, more generally. Watts has worked for UNDP, OECD and other development organizations, including the Ford, Rockefeller and MacArthur Foundations. He has published over fifteen books and three hundred articles and has worked extensively with the renowned photographer Ed Kashi. Watts has written extensively on the oil industry, extractive economies and international commodity trading firms.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Amy Weeks, Assistant Professor, University of Wisconsin, MadisonNew enzyme chemistry to decipher post-translational modification function Spatial organization and temporal dynamics are essential properties of cellular signaling. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins relay biological signals by exerting precise spatiotemporal control over protein function, localization, and lifetime. A systems-level experimental map of post-translationally modified proteins across subcellular space and time would transform our understanding of how PTMs orchestrate complex cellular functions in response to biological stimuli. However, such a map is inaccessible with current technologies. To meet this challenge, the Weeks lab is focused on developing new chemical and enzymatic tools for PTM proteomics with subcellular spatial and temporal resolution. We develop chemical probes and genetically targetable, PTM-selective proximity labeling enzymes to covalently tag post-translationally modified proteins in specific subcellular locations, enabling their enrichment and analysis with mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments. We focus on two pervasive PTMs, proteolysis and phosphorylation, both of which play critical roles in myriad biological signaling pathways relevant to human health and disease. Our technologies are broadly applicable to a wide variety of protease and kinase signaling pathways and provide an integrated view of cellular signaling with implications for both fundamental biological discovery and therapeutic innovation.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

Her first book, Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026), examines how a sovereign conception of the white patriarchal family was at the crux of an emerging conservative ideology opposed to the modern liberal state. The book is an extended version of her dissertation, which was awarded the 2019 Lerner-Scott Prize for the best dissertation in US women's history by the Organization of American Historians. She has held fellowships from the Jefferson Scholars Foundation, the Institute of Citizens and Scholars (formerly the Woodrow Wilson Institute), and, prior to joining the University of Melbourne, was an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong. She is now researching a project on the gendered politics of alternative health movements, including anti-vaccination, anti-fluoridation, and home birth movements, in the twentieth-century United States. *If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

Gil (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html)l, Professor of Anthropology at Towson University and an award-winning documentary filmmaker, based on his new book, Coming of Age in Macholand: Masculinity, Patriarchy, and the Search for Freedom in Indian Punjab (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand) (University of Chicago Press, forthcoming in Nov 2026), an eye-opening examination of masculinity, violence, and transnational migration focused on present-day Indian Punjab. Pre-order the book now. Only limited copies will be available to purchase at the event" - https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand). Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ���———–DATE: Tue, Dec 1, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKIn Coming of Age in Macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand), anthropologist and filmmaker Harjant Gill examines how Punjabi men in India, disillusioned by promises of power and control, contend with patriarchy: by submitting to it, attempting to transgress it, migrating to escape it, or coming undone by it. Gill takes readers deep inside men's worlds to show how boys come of age and how masculinity is produced through pervasive violence, while also being underwritten by intimacy, fraternal love, and homosocial bonds. Based on four years of fieldwork conducted over a decade and hundreds of interviews, Gill explores how boys learn to become men against the backdrop of patriarchal constraints, political violence, shifting agrarian economies, and steady outward migration. He shows the extent to which violence is a function and a reflection of powerlessness. By tracing the making of masculinity in a society where sexuality is sanctioned almost exclusively through heteronormative frameworks of marriage and family, this book documents how patriarchy forecloses agency and autonomy. Ultimately, Coming of Age in Macholand offers a powerful indictment of patriarchy as a system that not only oppresses women and queer people, but also constricts men's intimate, sexual, and emotional lives. ABOUT THE AUTHORHarjant Gill (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html) is a professor of anthropology and an award-winning documentary filmmaker whose work bridges ethnography, visual storytelling, and public scholarship. His research and creative practice explore masculinity, migration, media, religion, and popular culture in South Asia and its diasporas, with a particular focus on Punjab and Sikh communities. Through film and writing, he examines how intimate lives are shaped by patriarchy, nationalism, violence, and transnational mobility. Gill is the director of the internationally recognized documentary films Roots of Love, Mardistan/Macholand, and Sent Away Boys. His work has been broadcast on the BBC, PBS, and Doordarshan and screened widely at universities, film festivals, and public forums around the world. His scholarship appears in leading journals including American Anthropologist, Ethnography, and Visual Anthropology Review. His forthcoming book, Coming of Age in Macholand (University of Chicago Press), offers a deeply personal ethnographic exploration of patriarchy, masculinity, violence, and migration in Indian Punjab. Gill has received fellowships and awards from the American Institute of Indian Studies, Fulbright-Nehru, Point Foundation, Wenner-Gren, Whiting, and Woodrow Wilson foundations. Born in Chandigarh (India), Gill grew up in SF Bay Area and now lives in Washington, DC. events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Distinguished Lecture with Clifford Brangwynne, PhD
events.description: Fluid Machinery: The Nucleolus, Ribosomes, and Aging Abstract: Research combining insights from materials physics and cell biology has ushered in a new paradigm for understanding how the chaotic intracellular environment is brought to order, through the collective condensation of biomolecules into droplets of living information. In this talk, I will present an overview of these principles and ongoing work in this field, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between liquid-like condensates and traditional biomolecular machines, such as the ribosome, which forms through a complex assembly process in the multiphase nucleolus. Our lab has recently developed a set of tools to probe and engineer the nucleolus and the production of ribosomes, as well as their cytoplasmic function in protein translation. These studies are yielding new insights into how assembled ribosomes function in space and time, and how ribosomes can become dysregulated by molecular and organismal aging.

events.title: From dispersal to divergence: exploring the many faces of allopatric speciation
events.description: Freshwater fishes of eastern North America, particularly darters, are an exceptional system for studying the mechanisms and outcomes of allopatric speciation, given their high regional diversity and strong habitat specificity. Allopatric speciation is predicted to leave sister species in separate but adjacent river systems; yet a time-calibrated phylogeny of nearly all 290 darter species, combined with genomic species delimitation, reveals far more varied outcomes. Some sister lineages achieve secondary sympatry rapidly, while others persist in deep allopatry, never overlapping even with distant relatives, raising questions about why lineages differ in their transition rates from isolation to co-occurrence. At finer scales, case studies of recently delimited species complexes identify multiple drivers of allopatric speciation, including dispersal into newly available habitat and ecological divergence along resource axes like diet and substrate, extending well beyond classic vicariance models. This work establishes a research program linking speciation mechanisms to their long-term geographic and ecological consequences, contrasted with dynamics of island and lake adaptive radiations.

events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description: A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, December 3, 2026 (NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.Event Poster —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Myungji Yang (University of Hawai'i, Mānoa) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. She is the author of two books, From Miracle to Mirage (2018, Cornell University Press) and Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization (2026, Cambridge University Press). She is currently developing a research project on young men's radicalization and anti-feminist politics.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Stefan Minasian, Staff Chemist, LBNLThe Counterintuitive Relationship between Orbital Energy, Orbital Overlap,and Covalency in f-Element Molecules Why are some metal–ligand bonds more covalent than others? Typically, chemists invoke two factors: how well the metal and ligand orbitals overlap in space, and how closely their energies match. Yet these contributions have been surprisingly difficult to separate, by either experiment or theory. This lecture will describe how ligand K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), combined with high-level spectral simulations, can measure both. Comparisons of isostructural fluoride and chloride complexes of transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf), lanthanides (Ce), and actinides (U, Np, Pu) show that the two factors often work against each other. Greater orbital overlap does not necessarily produce a more covalent bond, and the balance between overlap and energy matching depends on the metal and on the symmetry of the interaction. These results also provide experimental benchmarks against which computational descriptions of bonding can be tested. The second part of the lecture will extend this approach to organometallic lanthanide complexes, probed using carbon K-edge XAS. In molecules such as cerocene, Ce(C8H8)2, and Cp′3Eu, the ground state cannot be described by a single electronic configuration. In these systems, the 4f orbital mixing observed by X-ray spectroscopy also appears as partial charge transfer from the ligands to the metal. Relating these two descriptions shows how 4f electrons can participate in bonding while remaining largely localized, and how 4f covalency can shape physical properties such as magnetic susceptibility. This leads to broader questions about how covalency and multiconfigurational ground states are connected across the f-block.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Lunch Poems: Bianca Stone
events.description: Lunch Poems (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/lunch-poems), Berkeley's storied noontime poetry series, welcomes Bianca Stone. Bianca Stone is the author of four collections of poetry. Her three most recent, all from Tin House Books, are The Near and Distant World (2026); What Is Otherwise Infinite (2022), winner of the 2022 Vermont Book Award; and The Möbius Strip Club of Grief (2018). Her work has appeared widely in such magazines as The New Yorker, The Atlantic, and Poetry. She is a visiting lecturer in poetry at Dartmouth College and teaches classes on poetry and poetic study at the Ruth Stone House in Goshen, Vermont, where she hosts the Ode & Psyche Podcast. Stone is currently serving as the poet laureate of Vermont (2024-28). The Lunch Poems series, founded by Professor Robert Hass, is supported by Dr. and Mrs. Tom Colby, the UC Berkeley Library, the Morrison Library Fund, the UC Berkeley English Department, and the Deans' Office of the College of Letters & Science. For more information or to be added to the Lunch Poems mailing list, please email poems-library@berkeley.edu (mailto:poems-library@berkeley.edu) or follow @PoemsLunch on Instagram (http://instagram.com/poemslunch) and X (https://twitter.com/PoemsLunch).

events.title: Genentech Lecture
events.description: Huw Davies, Asa Griggs Candler Professor, Harvard UniversitySite-selective and enantioselective C–H functionalization controlled by induced fitting and secondary noncovalent interactions A major challenge in organic synthesis is the selective functionalization of C–H bonds. As most organic compounds contain multiple C–H bonds with similar properties, distinguishing between them requires precise control. For some time, we have been using high symmetry chiral dirhodium catalysts to control C-H functionalization with donor acceptor carbenes. In this presentation we will highlight the design of our most recent high symmetry dirhodium catalysts (C4 symmetric and D4 symmetric) and illustrate the subtle site-selectivity exhibited by these catalysts. We will show how they can adopt many of the characteristics atypically associated with enzymes, leading to unprecedented site-selectivity of nonactivated C–H bonds. The catalysts adopt a bowl-shape on formation and the flexible microenvironment within the bowl causes an induced fitting to occur as the reagent and the substrate approach the catalyst. Recent synthetic application of this methodology to the synthesis of various chiral scaffolds will be described.

events.title: Shiben Banerji | Object, Site, Antecedent, Exemplar: India in the Occult Imagination of the Globe
events.description: A talk by Shiben Banerji, (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) Associate Professor of Architecture and Urbanism, History of Art Department, at UC Berkeley. ——–DATE: Thu, Mar 4, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ��———- SPEAKER BIOShiben Banerji (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) is Associate Professor in the Dept of History of Art. He interested in the rhetorical and performative dimensions of architecture. His classroom teaching and historical scholarship are animated by three questions. First, how did architects in early modern Europe describe their interest in the nature of political oratory at the very moment that they began studying architectural forms that were not derived from Roman antiquity? Second, how did architects across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia mediate new conceptions of public association in the context of nineteenth-century colonialisms, and how did concomitant experiments in old and new media present architectural and urban space as objects of artistic depiction and literary invention? Third, how did twentieth-century theorists of alternatives to liberal modernity in the ex-colonial world conceptualize the work of architectural media in altering perception and consciousness? Shiben is the author of Lineages of the Global City(link is external) (University of Texas Press, 2025), which was supported by a Mellon fellowship in the urban humanities and a publication grant from the Graham Foundation. Explicating the conjunction of planning and occultism in the early twentieth century, the book examines the designation of planned urban space as a site for forming a global ethos—meaning both an outlook on oneself as inescapably linked to every creature and thing, as well as the obligation to choose and act with a regard for one's inexorable impact on others. A similar attention to forms of rhetorical action that sustain notions of belonging informs Shiben's coedited volume In the Shadows of Democracy(link is external) (Intermezzo, 2025). Shiben is currently writing Time on the Road to Civil Rights, which foregrounds the salience of planning in civil rights discourse to advance a genealogical critique of the synchronic emergence of rhetorical theory and planning theory in the mid-twentieth century. He has also begun editing an anthology of uses and meanings of "spirit" in twentieth-century aesthetic, economic, and political thought. A dedicated teacher, Shiben was named Faculty of the Year by his students at the School of Art of Institute of Chicago when he was an Assistant Professor. To encourage new lines of graduate research, Shiben regularly contributes to Oxford Bibliographies in Architecture, Planning, and Preservation. ______ The South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) at the University of California, Berkeley promotes research-based conversations and collaborations around the arts of South Asia + its diasporas from the ancient period to the now. To read more about the Initiative and help support its various fundraising goals, please click HERE (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) ______ Event made possible with the support of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/sarah-kailath-chair-memorial-lecture) Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) The event is FREE and OPEN to the public.

events.title: Kamila Shamsie | The Mahomedali Habib Distinguished Lecture on Pakistan
events.description: The Institute and Pakistan@Berkeley (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/berkeley-pakistan-initiative), a campaign to broaden and deepen Pakistan related research, teaching and programming at UC Berkeley, are proud to announce the eleventh "Mahomedali Habib Distinguished Lecture on Pakistan (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/mahomedali-habib-lecture-series)" by the award winning writer and novelist, Kamila Shamsie (https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/697055/best-of-friends-by-kamila-shamsie/). Join us as the acclaimed Pakistani writer talks about her craft, and journey, and her latest novel, Best of Friends, with Harsha Ram (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/harsha-ram), Associate Professor in the Departments of Comparative Literature and of Slavic Languages and Literatures, UC Berkeley. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. _________________ This event will be live streamed on the Institute's FB page: ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) _________________Author Bio Kamila Shamsie is the author of eight novels, which have been translated into over 30 languages, including Burnt Shadows and A God in Every Stone. Her previous novel Home Fire won the Women's Prize for Fiction, was long listed for the Man Booker Prize and shortlisted for the Australian Book Industry Award for International Book. A Vice-President and Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature and Professor of Creative Writing at the University of Manchester, she was one of Granta's 'Best of Young British Novelists' in 2013. She grew up in Karachi, and now lives in London. Her new novel is Best of Friends, published in September 2022. _________________ Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) The event is FREE and OPEN to the public.

events.title: The Alan Dundes Lecture featuring Walter Rossa: "From Indo-Portuguese to Goan: the Role of Folk Expressions in Architecture"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: From Indo-Portuguese to Goan: the Role of Folk Expressions in Architecture In recent decades, scholarship on the Portuguese legacy in artistic expressions in Asia has hesitated to move beyond the global taxonomy of Indo-Portuguese, especially because of the difficulties of choosing or assuming the obvious terms on a case-by-case basis. Nationalisms, in the context of the nation-state crisis and religious-ethnic conflicts, are key clues to explaining this hesitation. Goan Catholic architecture is omnipresent in the promotional material of that fast-developing Indian state, an indisputable emblem of its brand and identity. What has defined its distinctive expression, its architectural grammar and discourse? In this lecture, I will present my contribution: between the colonial and the Goan, folk played a decisive role. Walter Rossa (Caracas, 1962), Architect (Lisbon, 1985), MA in History of Art (Lisbon, 1991), PhD and aggregated in Architecture (Coimbra, 2001 and 2013). Professor in the Department of Architecture and researcher at the Centre for the History of Society and Culture of the University of Coimbra. He holds the UNESCO Chair in Intercultural Dialogue in Heritages of Portuguese Influence (2019) and teaches courses in cultural heritage, town and regional planning, urban design, history, and architecture. Beyond his past work as a practising architect and town planner, he dedicated his efforts last year to cooperation and the relationship among heritage, history, planning, and development. He seeks to establish links between his academic work and development cooperation activities. A significant set of his publications is available at https://coimbra.academia.edu/WalterRossa

events.title: Ayesha S. ​Mahmud | Infectious Diseases in an Era of Global Change: Examples from Bangladesh
events.description: A talk by Ayesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud), Associate Professor of Demography, UC Berkeley on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally.Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, April 13, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) —————- ABSTRACT The ecological landscape of our planet is increasingly being shaped by a combination of global demographic shifts, such as rapid urbanization and increased human connectivity, and climatic changes, such as increases in mean temperatures and a greater frequency of extreme weather events. These global changes have important consequences for the emergence, evolution, geographic spread, and burden of infectious diseases. This talk will present insights from recent work on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally. SPEAKER BIOAyesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud) is an Associate Professor of Demography at UC Berkeley. Her research broadly examines the interplay between population change, environmental factors, and infectious disease dynamics. Drawing on theory and methods from demography and disease ecology, her work explores questions such as why outbreaks occur at particular times of year, how and why the mortality burden of infectious diseases changes over time, how population mobility shapes the spatial dynamics of outbreaks, and how global environmental and demographic change may alter patterns of infectious disease burden in the future. She uses statistical methods and biologically mechanistic models to investigate these questions across a range of diseases and settings in Asia, Africa, and Central America, drawing on data from disease surveillance systems, hospital databases, climate models, human mobility data, and population surveys and censuses. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Mahmud was a Rockefeller Foundation Planetary Health Fellow at Harvard University. She received her PhD in Demography from Princeton University in 2017.Event Poster TBA —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley)PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking in not always easily available in Berkeley. Take public transportation if possible or arrive early to secure your spot.DIRECTIONS (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/contactsdirections) We are located at 10 Stephens Hall on UC Berkeley's campus. Please click this Google Maps Link (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+Berkeley,+CA/@37.8712099,-122.3278764,12z/data=!4m9!4m8!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952!3e0) and enter your point of departure.

events.title: Ning Zheng: Molecular Glues: From Mechanisms to Therapeutics
events.description: Molecular glue (MG) degraders represent an exciting new modality in drug discovery highlighted by their ability to degrade undruggable targets and their favorable pharmacological properties. Thus far, only a very small number of MG degraders have been serendipitously found, most of which act on CULLIN4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. The scarcity of these novel compounds limits our understanding of their activity requirement, E3 ligases preference, and functional versatility, thereby hindering the prospective discovery of new MG degraders. In this presentation, I will highlight our latest studies on the identification of new MG degrader compounds as well as human disease mutations acting as genetic glues that foster neo-substrate-E3 interactions. These findings point to potential rational strategy for rational discovery of target-centric MG degraders.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: (Thomas Carell) Cynthia A. Chan Memorial Lecture: "The second dimension of the genetic code"
events.description: Cynthia A. Chan Memorial Lecture - DNA stores genetic information in the sequence of the four canonical bases dA, dC, dG, and T and, in addition, carries epigenetic information encoded by the four modified cytidine bases: 5-methylcytidine (mdC), 5-hydroxymethylcytidine (hmdC), 5-formylcytidine (fdC), and 5-carboxycytidine (cadC), with 5-hydroxymethyluridine (hmdU) potentially playing a role as well. These additional nucleosides are generated by TET(1–3) enzymes, which catalyze the stepwise oxidation of mdC or T to all the others, with the help of oxygen and -ketoglutarate. This oxidation chemistry in the genome thus establishes a second, largely uncharted layer of information. While the sequence code is static, the writing and erasure of the epigenetic code creates a dynamic information layer that controls gene activity, e.g. the differentiation of cells or memory formation and erasure in the brain. In this lecture, I will cover the discovery of the new epigenetic bases that expand the genetic alphabet using quantitative mass spectrometry and I will discuss new insights into their symmetry and localization based on recent sequencing data. I will then describe how the TET-based chemistry is now being exploited to develop new epigenetic sequencing methods that enable earlier cancer detection, thereby improving the chances of successful treatment. If time permits, I will also discuss why the modified base pseudouridine in mRNA allows the molecule to evade the innate immune system.
